title: Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire
body: Teaching at Oxford was happening by about 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world. Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, wasn't founded until 1325, more than two centuries later.

q.prompt: Which is older?

rq.prompt: Roughly when did teaching begin at Oxford?

why: Oxford's origins predate Tenochtitlan by over 200 years.

title: Cleopatra is closer to the Moon landing than the pyramids
body: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, about 2,500 years later. The Moon landing in 1969 was 'only' about 2,000 years after her.

q.prompt: Cleopatra lived closer in time to…
options: The building of the Great Pyramid

rq.prompt: About when was the Great Pyramid built?

why: Ancient Egypt lasted about 3,000 years; Cleopatra was near its end.

title: Mammoths outlived the first pyramids
body: Most woolly mammoths died out around 10,000 years ago, but a small population survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago. By then, Egypt's first pyramids had already been standing for centuries.

q.prompt: Were woolly mammoths still alive when Egypt's first pyramids were built?
options: No, they died out millions of years earlier

rq.prompt: Where did the last mammoths live?

why: Isolation on an island protected them from humans for longer.

title: Napoleon wasn't short
body: Napoleon was about 1.69 m (5 ft 7 in), average or slightly above for a Frenchman of his time. The myth grew from confusion between French and English inches, British cartoons mocking him, and his nickname 'le petit caporal', a term of affection.

q.prompt: How tall was Napoleon for his time?

rq.prompt: What helped create the 'short Napoleon' myth?

why: A French inch was longer than an English inch.

title: Vikings didn't wear horned helmets
body: No Viking-age helmet with horns has ever been found. The image largely comes from 19th-century art and costume designs, especially for Wagner's opera cycle The Ring of the Nibelung in 1876.

q.prompt: Did Vikings wear horned helmets in battle?

rq.prompt: Where did the horned-helmet image largely come from?

why: The only near-complete Viking helmet found has no horns.

title: You can't see the Great Wall from space
body: The Great Wall is very long but only a few metres wide, about the same colour as the land around it. Astronauts say it's essentially impossible to see with the naked eye from orbit, and certainly not from the Moon.

q.prompt: Is the Great Wall of China visible from the Moon?

rq.prompt: Why is the wall hard to see from orbit?
options: It's narrow and blends with the land

why: Width, not length, decides visibility from far away.

title: Romans cleaned clothes with urine
body: Roman laundries, called fullonicae, used stale urine because its ammonia helps lift grease and dirt. Urine was so useful that Emperor Vespasian taxed its collection. When his son objected, he reportedly said 'money doesn't stink'.

q.prompt: What did Roman laundries use to clean clothes?

rq.prompt: Which emperor taxed urine collection?

why: Ammonia in stale urine works as a cleaner.

title: The shortest war lasted under an hour
body: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 lasted roughly 38 to 45 minutes. British ships bombarded the palace after the new sultan refused to step down, and he soon fled. It's often called the shortest war in recorded history.

q.prompt: How long did the shortest recorded war last?

rq.prompt: Which war is often called the shortest in history?

why: Overwhelming naval firepower ended it almost immediately.

title: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be temporary
body: Built for the 1889 World's Fair, the Eiffel Tower had a 20-year permit and could have been dismantled in 1909. It was saved partly because it proved useful as a giant radio antenna.

q.prompt: What saved the Eiffel Tower from demolition?
options: Its use as a radio antenna

rq.prompt: How long was the tower's original permit?

why: Its height made it perfect for early radio transmitters.

title: The fax came before the telephone
body: Scottish inventor Alexander Bain patented an early fax-like machine in 1843, sending images over telegraph wires. Alexander Graham Bell's telephone patent came in 1876, over 30 years later.

q.prompt: Which was invented first?

rq.prompt: Who patented an early fax device in 1843?

why: Fax built on the telegraph, which already existed.

title: Nintendo started with playing cards
body: Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in 1889 to make hanafuda, traditional Japanese playing cards. It later tried taxis, instant rice and 'love hotels' before finding success with toys and video games.

q.prompt: What did Nintendo first make?

rq.prompt: When was Nintendo founded?

why: Hanafuda cards are still sold by Nintendo today.

title: Pyramid builders weren't slaves
body: Archaeologists found the village and tombs of the Giza pyramid workers. Evidence suggests they were paid labourers, fed bread, beer and meat, given medical care, and honoured with burials near the pyramids.

q.prompt: Who built the Giza pyramids, according to archaeology?

rq.prompt: What evidence shows the builders were respected?

why: Slaves wouldn't usually get honoured burials beside the king's tomb.

title: Medieval people knew Earth was round
body: Educated people in medieval Europe knew Earth was a sphere, as ancient Greeks had shown. The myth that they believed in a flat Earth was spread in the 1800s, partly by Washington Irving's romantic biography of Columbus.

q.prompt: Did educated medieval Europeans think Earth was flat?
options: No, they knew it was round

rq.prompt: Who helped spread the flat-Earth myth in the 1800s?

why: Ancient Greek scholars had shown Earth's roundness by about 330 BC.

source.name: Wikipedia: Myth of the flat Earth

title: The Great Fire of London recorded few deaths
body: The 1666 fire destroyed around 13,000 houses and 87 churches, including St Paul's Cathedral. Yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded. Historians think the real toll was higher, as poorer people's deaths often went unrecorded.

q.prompt: How many deaths were officially recorded in the Great Fire of London?

rq.prompt: Why might the true death toll be higher?

why: The fire spread slowly enough for many to flee.

title: The oldest recorded beer recipe is a poem
body: The Hymn to Ninkasi, a Sumerian poem written down around 1800 BC, praises the goddess of beer and describes how to brew it. It's one of the oldest known recipes in the world.

q.prompt: One of the oldest known recipes is for…

rq.prompt: Who was Ninkasi?

why: Writing it as a song helped people remember the steps.

title: The chess queen used to be weak
body: In early chess the queen, then called the vizier or counsellor, could move only one square diagonally. Around the late 1400s in Spain, the rules changed and she became the most powerful piece on the board.

q.prompt: How did the chess queen originally move?

rq.prompt: Where did the modern queen move first appear?

why: Faster games became popular, and the 'mad queen' rule spread.

title: Carrots weren't always orange
body: Early cultivated carrots were mostly purple or yellow. Orange varieties became common in the Netherlands in the 1600s. The popular story that Dutch growers bred them to honour William of Orange is unproven.

q.prompt: What colour were early cultivated carrots?

rq.prompt: Is it proven orange carrots honoured William of Orange?

why: Orange comes from beta-carotene, which growers selected for.

title: Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive
body: Marie Curie handled radium for years without knowing its dangers. Her notebooks are still contaminated more than a century later. They're kept in lead-lined boxes in Paris, and visitors sign a waiver and wear protective clothing.

q.prompt: How are Marie Curie's notebooks stored today?

rq.prompt: Why are her notebooks still dangerous?

why: Radium-226 has a half-life of about 1,600 years.

title: Rome's Pantheon dome still holds a record
body: The Pantheon's dome in Rome was completed around AD 125. Nearly 1,900 years later it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, with a 9-metre hole at the top open to the sky.

q.prompt: What record does Rome's Pantheon still hold?

rq.prompt: What's at the top of the Pantheon's dome?

why: Romans used lighter concrete higher up the dome to reduce weight.

title: Ancient Olympians competed naked
body: In the ancient Olympic Games, which began in 776 BC according to tradition, male athletes competed nude. The word gymnasium comes from the Greek gymnos, meaning naked.

q.prompt: What did ancient Olympic athletes wear?

rq.prompt: What does the Greek root of 'gymnasium' mean?

why: Nudity celebrated the human body and the gods.

title: Olympic gold medals are mostly silver
body: The last Olympic gold medals made of solid gold were awarded in 1912. Today's gold medals must be mostly silver, plated with at least 6 grams of gold.

q.prompt: What is a modern Olympic gold medal mostly made of?

rq.prompt: When were solid gold Olympic medals last awarded?

why: Solid gold medals would be very expensive.

title: Harvard is older than calculus
body: Harvard was founded in 1636. Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz developed calculus independently in the 1660s and 1670s. So Harvard's first students studied without it.

q.prompt: Which came first?

rq.prompt: Who developed calculus?

why: Universities predate many fields of modern maths.

title: Titanic had lifeboats for about half
body: Titanic carried 20 lifeboats with room for about 1,178 people, but around 2,224 were on board. That met the outdated rules of the time. After the 1912 disaster, new laws required lifeboat space for everyone.

q.prompt: How many people could Titanic's lifeboats hold?

rq.prompt: What changed after Titanic sank?
options: Icebergs were banned from shipping lanes

why: Old rules based lifeboats on ship weight, not passengers.

title: Sliced bread arrived in 1928
body: The first commercial bread-slicing machine was used in Chillicothe, Missouri, in 1928, invented by Otto Rohwedder. Ads called it 'the greatest forward step in the baking industry since bread was wrapped'.

q.prompt: When was sliced bread first sold?

rq.prompt: Who invented the bread-slicing machine?

why: Hence 'the best thing since sliced bread'.

title: The first flight was shorter than a jumbo jet
body: The Wright brothers' first powered flight in 1903 covered about 37 metres in 12 seconds. A Boeing 747's wingspan is about 64 metres, so the whole flight would fit along one jumbo jet's wings.

q.prompt: How far did the Wright brothers' first flight go?

rq.prompt: How long did the first powered flight last?

why: Short, but it was the first controlled, sustained powered flight.

title: The first computer bug was a real moth
body: In 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II computer found a moth trapped in a relay. They taped it into the logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found'. Engineers had already called glitches 'bugs', but this made the joke famous.

q.prompt: What was found inside the Harvard Mark II in 1947?

rq.prompt: Did the moth invent the word 'bug' for glitches?
options: It was named after a scientist called Bug

why: The logbook page is now at the Smithsonian.

title: The first webcam watched a coffee pot
body: In 1991, scientists at Cambridge University pointed a camera at the coffee pot in the Trojan Room so they could check if it was full without walking down the corridor. In 1993 it went on the web and became world famous.

q.prompt: What did the first webcam show?

rq.prompt: Where was the coffee pot webcam?

why: Saving a wasted trip for coffee was the whole point.

title: Velcro was inspired by burrs
body: Swiss engineer George de Mestral noticed burdock burrs clinging to his dog's fur after a walk in 1941. Under a microscope he saw tiny hooks catching on loops, and he spent years designing Velcro to copy them.

q.prompt: What inspired Velcro?

rq.prompt: How do burrs stick?

why: Copying nature in design is called biomimicry.

title: A melted snack led to the microwave oven
body: In 1945, engineer Percy Spencer was working on radar equipment when he noticed a sweet in his pocket had melted. He tested the effect on popcorn and an egg, and his company Raytheon went on to sell the first microwave ovens.

q.prompt: What tipped off the inventor of the microwave oven?
options: A melted sweet in his pocket

rq.prompt: What was Percy Spencer working on?

why: Radar uses microwaves, which heat water and fat molecules.

title: Penicillin came from a messy lab
body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find mould growing on one of his bacteria dishes. Around the mould, the bacteria had died. That mould produced penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic.

q.prompt: How was penicillin discovered?

rq.prompt: Who discovered penicillin?

why: Later work by Florey and Chain turned it into a medicine.

title: Post-it Notes came from a failed glue
body: In 1968, 3M scientist Spencer Silver was trying to make a super-strong glue and made a weak, reusable one instead. Years later, colleague Art Fry used it to stop bookmarks falling out of his choir hymnbook.

q.prompt: Post-it Notes came from an attempt to make…

rq.prompt: What problem did Art Fry want to solve?
options: Bookmarks falling out of a hymnbook

why: A 'failure' found the right problem later.

title: Coca-Cola once contained cocaine
body: Coca-Cola's original 1886 recipe used extract of coca leaves, which contain cocaine. The amount was cut sharply in 1903 and removed entirely by 1929. Today the company uses coca leaf extract with the cocaine taken out.

q.prompt: Did early Coca-Cola contain cocaine?

rq.prompt: By when was cocaine fully removed from Coca-Cola?

why: The 'Coca' in the name refers to the coca leaf.

title: The Statue of Liberty used to be brown
body: The Statue of Liberty is covered in thin copper sheets and was originally a shiny copper-brown. Over about 30 years, weathering formed a green layer called patina, which now protects the copper beneath.

q.prompt: What colour was the Statue of Liberty originally?

rq.prompt: What turned it green?

why: Copper reacts with air and water to form a green coating.

title: Big Ben is the bell
body: Big Ben is officially the nickname of the Great Bell inside the clock tower at Westminster, not the tower itself. The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 to mark Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.

q.prompt: What is 'Big Ben', strictly speaking?

rq.prompt: What is the tower's official name?

why: The bell's nickname spread to the whole tower.

title: Britain once skipped 11 days
body: To switch to the Gregorian calendar, Britain jumped from 2 September 1752 straight to 14 September. Much of Catholic Europe had already made the change in 1582, skipping 10 days.

q.prompt: What happened in Britain in September 1752?

rq.prompt: Which calendar did Britain switch to?

why: The old Julian calendar had slowly drifted from the seasons.

title: Royal purple came from sea snails
body: Tyrian purple, made from the glands of sea snails, took thousands of snails for a tiny amount of dye. It was so costly that in Rome, wearing it was a sign of the highest status, and some emperors restricted its use.

q.prompt: Where did the ancient world's royal purple dye come from?

rq.prompt: Why was purple dye so valuable?

why: Rarity made purple the colour of emperors.

title: A theft made the Mona Lisa famous
body: In 1911, Italian handyman Vincenzo Peruggia stole the Mona Lisa from the Louvre. It was missing for two years, and the headlines turned it into the world's most famous painting. Even Pablo Picasso was questioned by police.

q.prompt: What made the Mona Lisa world-famous in the 1910s?

rq.prompt: Which famous artist was questioned about the theft?

why: Two years of headlines made the painting a household name.

title: Einstein was offered Israel's presidency
body: In 1952, after Israel's first president died, the prime minister offered the largely ceremonial presidency to Albert Einstein. He declined, saying he lacked the aptitude and experience to deal with people and official duties.

q.prompt: What job was Einstein offered in 1952?

rq.prompt: What did Einstein say to the offer?

why: He felt he lacked the skills for politics.

title: Isaac Newton hunted counterfeiters
body: Late in life, Isaac Newton ran England's Royal Mint. He took the job seriously, personally investigating forgers and gathering evidence, and some of the counterfeiters he pursued were executed.

q.prompt: What job did Isaac Newton hold later in life?

rq.prompt: Who did Newton pursue at the Mint?

why: Fake coins were a serious threat to the economy.

title: Ada Lovelace wrote an early computer program
body: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine. They included a step-by-step method for calculating Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program, a century before computers existed.

q.prompt: Who is often credited with the first published computer program?

rq.prompt: For which machine did she write it?

why: She saw the machine could manipulate symbols, not just numbers.

title: The Rosetta Stone cracked hieroglyphs
body: The Rosetta Stone, carved in 196 BC, records the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and ancient Greek. Scholars could read the Greek, and in 1822 Jean-François Champollion used it to decode hieroglyphs.

q.prompt: Why was the Rosetta Stone so important?

rq.prompt: Who deciphered hieroglyphs in 1822?

why: The known Greek text unlocked the unknown hieroglyphs.

title: Stonehenge's stones travelled far
body: Stonehenge's smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, about 240 km away. In 2024, scientists showed its central Altar Stone came from northeast Scotland, over 700 km away. How they were moved is still debated.

q.prompt: Where did Stonehenge's Altar Stone come from?

rq.prompt: Where are the bluestones from?

why: Chemical fingerprints in the rock match their source.

title: Pompeii's walls are full of graffiti
body: When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in AD 79, it preserved thousands of graffiti scrawled on walls: election slogans, insults, jokes, love notes and adverts. They give a rare glimpse of everyday Roman life.

q.prompt: What did Vesuvius preserve on Pompeii's walls?

rq.prompt: When was Pompeii buried?

why: Ash sealed the city, protecting it for centuries.

title: A Greek measured Earth with shadows
body: Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes compared the angle of shadows at noon in two Egyptian cities a known distance apart. Using simple geometry, he estimated Earth's circumference remarkably close to the real value of about 40,000 km.

q.prompt: How did Eratosthenes measure Earth?

rq.prompt: About when did he do it?

why: Different shadow angles reveal Earth's curve.

title: An ancient Greek 'computer' predicted eclipses
body: The Antikythera mechanism, found in a shipwreck in 1901, is a box of bronze gears made over 2,000 years ago. It modelled the movements of the Sun and Moon and predicted eclipses. Nothing as complex is known for another thousand years.

q.prompt: What could the Antikythera mechanism do?

rq.prompt: Where was it found?

why: Its interlocking gears mirrored the cycles of the sky.

title: Hadrian's Wall crossed Britain
body: Started around AD 122 on Emperor Hadrian's orders, the wall ran about 118 km across northern England, from coast to coast. It had forts and milecastles along its length. Much of it is still standing.

q.prompt: Who ordered a wall across northern Britain in AD 122?

rq.prompt: About how long was Hadrian's Wall?

why: It marked and controlled the empire's northern frontier.

title: The Black Death killed up to half of Europe
body: Between 1347 and 1351 the Black Death, caused by plague bacteria spread by fleas and people, killed an estimated 30 to 60% of Europe's population. It took centuries for the population to recover.

q.prompt: What share of Europe died in the Black Death?
options: Roughly a third to a half

rq.prompt: What caused the Black Death?

why: Crowded towns and trade routes helped it spread fast.

title: Tulip mania may be exaggerated
body: In 1630s Holland, rare tulip bulbs sold for huge sums before prices crashed in 1637. It's often called the first financial bubble. Some historians now argue the damage to the wider economy was much smaller than popular stories claim.

q.prompt: What crashed in Holland in 1637?

rq.prompt: What do some modern historians say about tulip mania?

why: Later moralising writers spread the dramatic version.

title: London built the first underground railway
body: The Metropolitan Railway opened in London in 1863, the world's first underground railway. Its trains were pulled by steam engines, which filled the tunnels with smoke.

q.prompt: Which city had the world's first underground railway?

rq.prompt: What powered the first Tube trains?

why: Tunnels were dug just under streets using 'cut and cover'.

title: Saint Patrick wasn't Irish
body: Saint Patrick was born in Roman Britain in the 5th century. At about 16 he was captured by raiders and taken to Ireland as a slave. He escaped, later returned as a missionary, and became Ireland's patron saint.

q.prompt: Where was Saint Patrick born?

rq.prompt: How did Patrick first come to Ireland?

why: His own writings describe his capture and escape.

title: Joan of Arc was a teenager
body: Joan of Arc was about 17 when she helped lift the siege of Orléans in 1429, leading French troops in the Hundred Years' War. She was captured, tried for heresy and burned at the stake in 1431, aged around 19.

q.prompt: About how old was Joan of Arc when she died?

rq.prompt: Which siege did Joan help lift in 1429?

why: She was declared a saint in 1920.

title: The Mongols built the largest connected empire
body: Founded by Genghis Khan in 1206, the Mongol Empire grew to stretch from Korea to eastern Europe. At its height it was the largest contiguous land empire in history, linked by a fast horseback postal relay.

q.prompt: What was the largest connected land empire ever?

rq.prompt: Who founded the Mongol Empire?

why: Mounted archers let the Mongols conquer vast distances quickly.

title: Machu Picchu was never lost to locals
body: Machu Picchu was built around 1450 for the Inca ruler Pachacuti. When American explorer Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911, local farmers were living there and guided him up. It was 'lost' only to the outside world.

q.prompt: Was Machu Picchu truly lost before 1911?

rq.prompt: Who was Machu Picchu built for?

why: Its remote location kept the Spanish from finding it.

title: Easter Island heads have bodies
body: Many of the famous moai statues on Easter Island (Rapa Nui) look like giant heads, but excavations show some have full torsos buried underground by centuries of soil. Some buried bodies even carry carvings.

q.prompt: What's hidden below many Easter Island 'heads'?

rq.prompt: What buried the moai bodies?

why: Erosion from the hills slowly buried the statues on slopes.

title: People danced for days in 1518
body: In July 1518 in Strasbourg, a woman began dancing in the street and couldn't stop. Over weeks, dozens more joined in. Authorities even hired musicians, thinking more dancing would cure it. The cause is still debated.

q.prompt: What happened in Strasbourg in 1518?

rq.prompt: How did the authorities first respond?

why: Historians suggest stress-induced mass hysteria.

title: Australia lost a war to emus
body: In 1932, Australian soldiers with machine guns were sent to cull emus damaging crops in Western Australia. The fast, scattered birds proved very hard to hit, and the operation was called off having failed to solve the problem.

q.prompt: Who 'won' Australia's 1932 Emu War?

rq.prompt: Why were soldiers sent after emus?

why: Emus can run about 50 km/h and scatter in all directions.

title: A molasses flood hit Boston
body: In January 1919, a huge tank of molasses burst in Boston. A wave of syrup several metres high rushed through the streets, killing 21 people. Locals claimed the area smelled sweet on hot days for decades.

q.prompt: What flooded part of Boston in 1919?

rq.prompt: How many people died in the molasses flood?

why: Molasses is thick and heavy, and trapped people as it cooled.

title: A stink gave London its sewers
body: In the hot summer of 1858, the sewage-filled River Thames smelled so bad that Parliament struggled to work. The 'Great Stink' pushed MPs to fund Joseph Bazalgette's sewer network, which still serves London today.

q.prompt: What pushed Parliament to build London's sewers?
options: A terrible smell from the Thames

rq.prompt: Who engineered London's sewer system?

why: The system also helped end London's cholera outbreaks.

title: The 1904 Olympic marathon was chaos
body: At the 1904 St Louis Olympics, the first man to finish had ridden part of the way in a car and was disqualified. The winner, Thomas Hicks, was kept going by his team with doses of strychnine and brandy, a dangerous mix.

q.prompt: How did the first finisher of the 1904 marathon cheat?
options: He took a shortcut by boat

rq.prompt: What was the real winner given during the race?

why: There were almost no rules on doping then.

source.name: Wikipedia: Athletics at the 1904 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon

title: The oldest recorded joke is about a fart
body: A Sumerian proverb from around 1900 BC is often listed as the oldest recorded joke. It's a quip about something that has never happened since time began, involving a young woman and breaking wind.

q.prompt: What is the world's oldest recorded joke about?

rq.prompt: Which civilisation recorded it?

why: Toilet humour turns out to be ancient.

title: The oldest university may be in Morocco
body: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez was founded as a mosque and school in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri. UNESCO and Guinness World Records list it as the oldest existing, continually operating educational institution in the world.

q.prompt: Who founded the University of al-Qarawiyyin?

rq.prompt: Where is al-Qarawiyyin?

why: She used her inheritance to fund it.

title: China invented paper money
body: Merchants in Song dynasty China began using paper notes in the 11th century because heavy iron coins were awkward to carry. The government soon took over printing them, centuries before paper money caught on in Europe.

q.prompt: Where was paper money first widely used?

rq.prompt: Why did Chinese merchants want paper money?

why: Paper was light and printing was already advanced in China.

title: Gunpowder came from a search for immortality
body: Chinese alchemists in the 800s, mixing saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal while searching for an elixir of life, discovered a mixture that burned violently instead. It became gunpowder, first used in fireworks and later in weapons.

q.prompt: What were the inventors of gunpowder looking for?

rq.prompt: What three ingredients make black gunpowder?

why: Saltpetre provides oxygen, letting it burn incredibly fast.

title: Movable type predates Gutenberg
body: Around 1040, Chinese inventor Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay. Korea later printed books with metal movable type, including a surviving 1377 book. Gutenberg's press in Germany came around 1440.

q.prompt: Who first invented movable type?

rq.prompt: What was Bi Sheng's type made of?

why: Gutenberg's big advance was combining type with a press and oil inks for mass printing.

title: Gandhi walked 390 km for salt
body: In 1930, Mahatma Gandhi led a 24-day march of about 390 km to the sea to make salt, breaking British laws that taxed it. The Salt March drew worldwide attention to India's independence movement.

q.prompt: What did Gandhi march to the sea to make?

rq.prompt: About how long was the Salt March?

why: Making salt was a simple act anyone could join.

title: The Berlin Wall fell after a press slip
body: On 9 November 1989, East German spokesman Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules, and when asked when they started, said 'immediately'. He hadn't been briefed properly. Crowds rushed the border, and guards opened the gates.

q.prompt: What helped trigger the fall of the Berlin Wall?

rq.prompt: What word did Schabowski use for when the rules started?

why: Live TV spread the news before officials could correct it.

source.name: Wikipedia: Fall of the Berlin Wall

title: Apollo 11's computer had about 4 KB of memory
body: The Apollo Guidance Computer that helped land astronauts on the Moon had about 2,048 words of working memory, roughly 4 kilobytes. A modern phone has millions of times more.

q.prompt: Roughly how much working memory did Apollo 11's computer have?

rq.prompt: What was the Apollo Guidance Computer used for?

why: Clever, efficient programs made every bit count.

title: Only one ancient wonder survives
body: Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, only the Great Pyramid of Giza still stands. The others, including the Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, were destroyed, or, in the gardens' case, may never have existed.

q.prompt: Which of the Seven Ancient Wonders still stands?

rq.prompt: Which wonder may never have existed?

why: Earthquakes, fires and looting took the others.

source.name: Wikipedia: Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

title: A film star helped invent Wi-Fi's ancestor
body: In 1942, Hollywood actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil patented 'frequency hopping', a way to stop enemies jamming radio-guided torpedoes. Similar spread-spectrum ideas later fed into Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS.

q.prompt: Which actress co-invented frequency hopping?

rq.prompt: What was frequency hopping first meant to protect?

why: Switching frequencies quickly makes signals hard to jam.

title: Scotland's national animal is a unicorn
body: The unicorn has been a Scottish heraldic symbol since the 1100s, standing for purity and power. On the UK royal coat of arms, it faces England's lion. In legend, the unicorn is so wild it has to be chained.

q.prompt: What is Scotland's national animal?

rq.prompt: Which animal faces the unicorn on the royal coat of arms?

why: Medieval legends made the unicorn a symbol of untamed strength.

source.name: Wikipedia: Royal coat of arms of the United Kingdom

title: The monarch gets two birthdays
body: Britain's monarch has an actual birthday and an official one, usually celebrated in June with the Trooping the Colour parade. The tradition took hold in the 1700s, largely because summer weather suits a parade far better.

q.prompt: Why does the British monarch have an official birthday?

rq.prompt: What parade marks the official birthday?

why: Ceremonial outdoor events are easier in June.

title: Romans had fast-food counters
body: Pompeii had dozens of thermopolia, street counters selling hot food and drink. In 2020 archaeologists uncovered one with painted animals, traces of duck, pork and snail, and jars still set into the counter.

q.prompt: What was a Roman thermopolium?

rq.prompt: Which food traces were found in Pompeii's counter?

why: Many poorer Romans had no kitchen at home.

title: France used the guillotine until 1977
body: The guillotine, adopted during the French Revolution in 1792, remained France's method of execution for nearly two centuries. The last execution was in 1977, the same year Star Wars came out. France abolished the death penalty in 1981.

q.prompt: When was the guillotine last used in France?

rq.prompt: When did France abolish the death penalty?

why: It was intended as a quicker, more 'humane' method at the time.

title: Fanta was born in wartime Germany
body: During the Second World War, Coca-Cola's German branch couldn't get the syrup for Coke. In 1940 it invented a new drink from available leftovers like whey and apple pulp, and called it Fanta, from 'Fantasie'.

q.prompt: Why was Fanta invented?
options: Coke syrup couldn't reach wartime Germany

rq.prompt: What word does 'Fanta' come from?

why: Trade embargoes cut off Coca-Cola's ingredients.

title: Jeans got rivets in 1873
body: Tailor Jacob Davis put copper rivets on work trousers to stop pockets tearing. He partnered with fabric supplier Levi Strauss, and they patented riveted denim in 1873, the birth of blue jeans.

q.prompt: Why were rivets added to jeans?

rq.prompt: Who first came up with riveted jeans?

why: Miners needed tough clothes.

title: 1816 was the year without a summer
body: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia threw so much ash into the sky that 1816 brought snow in June in parts of North America and failed harvests across Europe. Stuck indoors that gloomy summer, Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein.

q.prompt: Which novel was born in the 'year without a summer'?

rq.prompt: What caused the cold of 1816?

why: Volcanic particles in the stratosphere reflect sunlight.

title: Krakatoa was heard 4,800 km away
body: When Krakatoa erupted in 1883, the explosion was heard on an island near Mauritius, about 4,800 km away. It's often called the loudest sound in recorded history, and pressure waves circled the globe several times.

q.prompt: How far away was Krakatoa's 1883 eruption heard?

rq.prompt: What did Krakatoa's pressure waves do?

why: The explosion was one of the most powerful in history.

title: Tutankhamun's tomb was found nearly intact
body: In 1922, Howard Carter found the tomb of the young pharaoh Tutankhamun in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Most royal tombs had been robbed, but this one still held over 5,000 objects, including the famous gold mask.

q.prompt: Why was Tutankhamun's tomb such a big find?

rq.prompt: Who found the tomb in 1922?

why: Its entrance was hidden by debris from a later tomb.

title: The Library of Alexandria faded slowly
body: The popular story has the great library destroyed in one dramatic fire. Historians think it declined over centuries through funding cuts, political purges, war damage and neglect. Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BC did harm, but the library survived it.

q.prompt: How did the Library of Alexandria end, most historians think?

rq.prompt: Did the library survive Julius Caesar's fire?

why: Losing support and scholars was more damaging than any single fire.

title: Ancient Egyptians revered cats
body: Cats were linked to the goddess Bastet in ancient Egypt, and many were mummified. The Greek historian Diodorus reported a Roman who accidentally killed a cat being lynched by an angry crowd.

q.prompt: Which goddess were cats linked with in ancient Egypt?

rq.prompt: What did Egyptians often do with cats after death?

why: Cats protected grain stores from mice and snakes.

title: Pineapples were 18th-century status symbols
body: In 1700s Britain, pineapples had to be grown in heated hothouses or imported, and cost a fortune. They became symbols of wealth: they appear carved on buildings, and some people reportedly rented one just to show off at a party.

q.prompt: What did pineapples symbolise in 1700s Britain?

rq.prompt: How were pineapples grown in Britain?

why: Rarity and cost made them luxury displays.

title: The printing press spread the Reformation
body: When Martin Luther published his 95 Theses in 1517, printing presses copied his arguments fast. Within weeks his ideas spread across Germany, and printed pamphlets helped the Protestant Reformation grow faster than earlier church reform movements.

q.prompt: What technology helped Luther's ideas spread fast?

rq.prompt: When did Luther publish his 95 Theses?

why: Earlier reformers relied on handwritten copies and preaching.

title: The first photo of a person was an accident
body: In 1838, Louis Daguerre photographed a busy Paris boulevard. The exposure took several minutes, so moving traffic vanished. But a man stood still having his boots shined, making him likely the first person ever photographed.

q.prompt: Why does Daguerre's busy 1838 street photo look empty?

rq.prompt: Who was likely the first person photographed?
options: A man getting his boots shined

why: Long exposures only capture things that stay still.

title: The QWERTY layout is from typewriters
body: Christopher Latham Sholes developed the QWERTY layout in the 1870s for early typewriters. One popular explanation is that it separated common letter pairs to reduce jams. Despite better layouts since, QWERTY stuck because everyone had learned it.

q.prompt: Where does the QWERTY keyboard layout come from?

rq.prompt: Why has QWERTY lasted?

why: Switching costs keep old standards alive.

title: The longest-reigning monarch ruled 72 years
body: Louis XIV of France became king in 1643 aged four and reigned until 1715, about 72 years. That's the longest recorded reign of any monarch of a sovereign country. Elizabeth II reigned 70 years.

q.prompt: Who reigned longest of any sovereign monarch?

rq.prompt: How old was Louis XIV when he became king?

why: Starting very young is the key to a record reign.

title: Ancient Egyptians used a 365-day calendar
body: The ancient Egyptians had a civil calendar of 365 days: twelve months of 30 days plus five extra days. They tied their year to the yearly flood of the Nile. Our calendar descends partly from it, via the Romans.

q.prompt: How many days were in the ancient Egyptian civil year?

rq.prompt: What natural event anchored Egypt's year?

why: Farming depended on predicting the flood.

title: Queen Victoria survived several assassination attempts
body: Queen Victoria faced at least seven attempts on her life during her reign. None succeeded, and each one tended to boost her popularity with the public.

q.prompt: How many assassination attempts did Queen Victoria survive?

rq.prompt: What effect did the attempts have on her popularity?

why: Public sympathy rallied around the monarch.

title: The Wild West wasn't so deadly
body: Western cattle towns had far fewer killings than films suggest. One historian counted 15 homicides in Dodge City across its busiest decade, 1876 to 1885. The famous Gunfight at the O.K. Corral in Tombstone lasted about 30 seconds.

q.prompt: How long did the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral last?

rq.prompt: Were Wild West towns as deadly as films show?

why: Many towns banned carrying guns within town limits.

title: The Great Pyramid was the tallest for 3,800 years
body: Built around 2560 BC, the Great Pyramid of Giza was originally about 146 metres tall. It remained the tallest human-made structure in the world for over 3,800 years, until Lincoln Cathedral's spire overtook it in the early 1300s.

q.prompt: What overtook the Great Pyramid as the tallest structure?

rq.prompt: About how tall was the Great Pyramid originally?

why: Its outer casing stones were later removed, lowering it.

title: Lincoln Cathedral's spire collapsed in 1548
body: Lincoln Cathedral's central spire took the title of world's tallest structure from the Great Pyramid in the 1300s, rising about 160 metres. It held that record for over 200 years until the spire blew down in a storm in 1548.

q.prompt: What ended Lincoln Cathedral's record?

rq.prompt: Which country is Lincoln Cathedral in?

why: Tall wooden and lead spires were vulnerable to storms.

title: Timbuktu was a great centre of learning
body: In the 1300s to 1500s, Timbuktu in Mali was a wealthy trading city and a major centre of Islamic scholarship. Its families kept hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on astronomy, law, medicine and maths, many still preserved today.

q.prompt: What was medieval Timbuktu famous for?

rq.prompt: Which modern country is Timbuktu in?

why: Trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt brought wealth and scholars.

title: Mansa Musa may be history's richest person
body: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire in the 1300s, when it produced much of the world's gold. On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, he gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value fell there for years.

q.prompt: What happened when Mansa Musa visited Cairo in 1324?

rq.prompt: Which empire did Mansa Musa rule?

why: Flooding a market with gold lowers its price.

title: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years
body: The Hundred Years' War between England and France ran from 1337 to 1453, about 116 years. It wasn't continuous fighting but a series of wars and truces over claims to the French throne.

q.prompt: How long did the Hundred Years' War actually last?

rq.prompt: Which two countries fought it?

why: Historians named it later, rounding the length.

title: Lego bricks from 1958 still fit today
body: Lego patented its stud-and-tube brick design in 1958. Bricks made then still click together with ones made today, because the company has kept the dimensions precise to tiny fractions of a millimetre.

q.prompt: Will a 1958 Lego brick fit a new one?

rq.prompt: When was the modern Lego brick patented?

why: Tight manufacturing tolerances keep 'clutch power' the same.

title: Ancient Romans had a fire brigade
body: In AD 6, Emperor Augustus created the Vigiles, a force of freedmen that grew to around 7,000, who fought fires and patrolled Rome's streets at night. They used buckets, pumps, axes and blankets soaked in vinegar.

q.prompt: Who were Rome's Vigiles?

rq.prompt: Which emperor set up the Vigiles?

why: Crowded wooden housing made fire a constant danger.

title: Ketchup was once sold as medicine
body: In the 1830s, an American doctor named John Cook Bennett promoted tomato ketchup as a cure for indigestion and other ailments. Tomato 'pills' became a fad before the claims were exposed as nonsense.

q.prompt: How was tomato ketchup promoted in the 1830s?

rq.prompt: What happened to the tomato pill craze?

why: Patent medicines were largely unregulated then.

title: Abraham Lincoln is in the wrestling hall of fame
body: As a young man, Abraham Lincoln was a skilled wrestler, reportedly losing only one of around 300 matches. In 1992 he was honoured by the US National Wrestling Hall of Fame.

q.prompt: What sport was Abraham Lincoln known for as a young man?

rq.prompt: How many matches did Lincoln reportedly lose?

why: Frontier wrestling was a popular contest of strength.

title: The Colosseum could be flooded, perhaps
body: Ancient writers describe mock sea battles staged in Rome's Colosseum. Historians think early in its life the arena may have been flooded for shows, before the underground rooms and lifts were built under the floor.

q.prompt: What might the Colosseum have been flooded for?

rq.prompt: What later made flooding impossible?
options: Underground rooms built below the arena

why: The hypogeum's tunnels and lifts filled the space below the floor.

title: The first speeding ticket was for 8 mph
body: In 1896, Walter Arnold of Kent was fined for driving at about 8 mph in a 2 mph zone, often cited as the world's first speeding conviction. British law then also required a person to walk ahead of some vehicles.

q.prompt: How fast was the first speeding driver going?

rq.prompt: What was the speed limit he broke?

why: Early motoring laws treated cars like slow steam engines.

title: Alexander the Great never lost a battle
body: Alexander the Great became king of Macedon at 20 and by 32 had built an empire from Greece to India. Ancient historians record no defeat in a major battle. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32.

q.prompt: How old was Alexander the Great when he died?

rq.prompt: Where did Alexander die?

why: His speed and tactics overwhelmed much larger armies.

title: Microwaves don't cook from the inside out
body: Microwave ovens make water molecules in food jiggle, which heats it. The waves only penetrate a few centimetres, so the outer layers heat first and the heat spreads inward by conduction. That's why thick food can stay cold in the middle.

q.prompt: How does a microwave oven heat food?
options: Jiggles water molecules near the surface

rq.prompt: Why can the middle of thick food stay cold?
options: Microwaves only reach a few cm in

why: Stirring or resting lets heat spread evenly.

title: Touchscreens feel your electricity
body: Most phone screens are capacitive: a grid of tiny electrodes holds an electric field. Your finger conducts electricity and disturbs the field at that spot. Ordinary gloves block this, which is why they don't work on screens.

q.prompt: Why don't touchscreens work with ordinary gloves?
options: Gloves block your body's electrical effect

rq.prompt: What do capacitive screens detect?

why: Touchscreen gloves have conductive threads in the fingertips.

title: Noise-cancelling fights sound with sound
body: Noise-cancelling headphones use microphones to listen to the noise around you, then play a sound wave that is its exact mirror image. The peaks of one meet the troughs of the other, and they largely cancel out.

q.prompt: How do noise-cancelling headphones work?
options: They play an opposite sound wave

rq.prompt: Which noises are easiest to cancel?

why: Predictable sounds are easy to mirror in time.

title: GPS needs Einstein to work
body: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks. Because of relativity, their clocks run about 38 microseconds a day faster than clocks on the ground. Without correcting for that, GPS positions would drift by kilometres every day.

q.prompt: What would happen to GPS without relativity corrections?
options: It would drift by kilometres a day

rq.prompt: How much faster do GPS satellite clocks run each day?

why: Weaker gravity and high speed both change how fast time passes.

title: GPS works by timing signals
body: Your phone doesn't send anything to GPS satellites. It listens for time signals from at least four of them and calculates how far away each one is from how long the signal took. Combining the distances pins down your position.

q.prompt: Does your phone send signals to GPS satellites?

rq.prompt: How many satellites does a GPS fix need at minimum?

why: Three give position; the fourth corrects your phone's clock.

title: Fridges pump heat out
body: A fridge doesn't make cold; it moves heat. A refrigerant liquid evaporates inside, soaking up heat, then a compressor squeezes it so it releases that heat through coils at the back. That's why the back of a fridge feels warm.

q.prompt: Why is the back of a fridge warm?
options: It dumps heat taken from inside

rq.prompt: What soaks up heat inside a fridge?

why: Evaporation absorbs heat, the same way sweat cools you.

title: The 'equal time' wing explanation is wrong
body: A common explanation says air over a wing's curved top must reach the back at the same time as air below, so it speeds up. It doesn't: top air actually arrives first. Wings make lift by turning air downward, creating lower pressure above.

q.prompt: Does air over a wing reach the back at the same time as air below?

rq.prompt: How do wings really make lift?

why: Pushing air down pushes the wing up.

title: Why the sky is blue
body: Sunlight contains every colour. As it passes through air, tiny gas molecules scatter short blue wavelengths much more than red ones. That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from all over the sky.

q.prompt: Why is the sky blue?

rq.prompt: Why are sunsets red?
options: Light passes through more air, scattering away blue

why: This is called Rayleigh scattering.

title: Card chips make a one-time code
body: When you pay with a chip card, the chip generates a unique code for that one transaction using a secret key that never leaves the card. A copied code is useless for another payment, which is why chips cut card cloning.

q.prompt: What does your bank card chip create for each payment?
options: Nothing, it just stores your number

rq.prompt: Why can't criminals reuse a copied chip code?

why: Magnetic stripes repeated the same data, so they were easy to clone.

title: Contactless works within about 4 cm
body: Contactless payment uses near-field communication (NFC). The reader's magnetic field powers the card's chip and exchanges data, but only over very short distances, typically up to about 4 cm.

q.prompt: How close must a contactless card usually be?

rq.prompt: What powers a contactless card's chip?

why: The short range is a deliberate security feature.

title: QR codes survive damage
body: QR codes contain built-in error correction. At the highest setting, up to about 30% of a code can be dirty, torn or covered by a logo and it will still scan correctly.

q.prompt: How much of a QR code can be damaged and still scan?

rq.prompt: Why can logos sit in the middle of QR codes?
options: Error correction fills in missing parts

why: Extra redundant data lets the scanner rebuild missing bits.

title: Barcodes check themselves
body: The last digit of a standard product barcode is a check digit, worked out by a simple sum of the other digits. If the scanner misreads a number, the sum won't match and it rejects the scan instead of charging for the wrong item.

q.prompt: What is the last digit of a product barcode for?

rq.prompt: What happens if a barcode check doesn't match?

why: A cheap calculation catches most misreads.

title: Wi-Fi and microwaves share a frequency
body: Many Wi-Fi networks use the 2.4 GHz radio band, the same region microwave ovens use to heat food. Ovens are shielded, but a little leakage can slow Wi-Fi while someone heats lunch.

q.prompt: Which kitchen appliance can interfere with Wi-Fi?

rq.prompt: Which frequency band do they share?

why: The 2.4 GHz band is open for anyone to use without a licence.

title: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king
body: Bluetooth is named after Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson, a 10th-century king who united Danish tribes. The tech was meant to unite devices. Its logo combines the runes for his initials, H and B.

q.prompt: Who is Bluetooth named after?

rq.prompt: What does the Bluetooth logo show?

why: Uniting tribes became a metaphor for uniting gadgets.

title: The @ in email was a quick choice
body: In 1971, engineer Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked email between two computers. He picked @ to separate the user from the computer's name because it was on the keyboard and didn't appear in names.

q.prompt: Why did Ray Tomlinson choose @ for email?

rq.prompt: When was the first networked email sent?

why: 'user at computer' read naturally.

title: Long passwords beat clever ones
body: Each extra character multiplies the guesses an attacker needs. A long passphrase of several random words is usually harder to crack than a short jumble like 'P@55w0rd!', and easier to remember. Modern security guidance favours length.

q.prompt: Which is usually stronger?

rq.prompt: Why does length matter so much?

why: Attackers guess common substitutions like @ for a.

title: The padlock doesn't mean a site is safe
body: The padlock in your browser means your connection is encrypted, so others can't read the data in transit. It doesn't prove the website is honest; scam sites can have padlocks too.

q.prompt: What does the browser padlock mean?

rq.prompt: Can scam sites show a padlock?

why: Encryption certificates are free and easy to get.

title: Incognito mode hides less than you think
body: Private browsing stops your browser saving history and cookies on your device. Websites, your employer or school network, and your internet provider can still see what you visit.

q.prompt: Who can still see your visits in incognito mode?

rq.prompt: What does incognito mode actually stop?

why: It's privacy from others using your device, not from the internet.

title: Heat ages phone batteries
body: Lithium-ion batteries wear out faster when hot or kept at full charge for long periods. That's why many phones now pause charging around 80% overnight. Leaving a phone in a hot car is one of the worst things for its battery.

q.prompt: What wears out phone batteries fastest?

rq.prompt: Why do phones pause charging around 80% overnight?

why: Heat and high charge speed up chemical side-reactions.

title: The Rule of 72
body: To estimate how long it takes money to double with compound interest, divide 72 by the yearly interest rate. At 6% a year, money doubles in about 12 years. At 9%, about 8 years.

q.prompt: Roughly how long does money take to double at 6% a year?

rq.prompt: What's the Rule of 72 used for?

why: Compound growth earns interest on past interest.

title: Banks create most money by lending
body: Most money in a modern economy isn't notes and coins but bank deposits. The Bank of England explains that when a bank makes a loan, it creates a new deposit in the borrower's account, effectively creating new money.

rq.prompt: What happens when a bank makes a loan?

why: The Bank of England described this in a 2014 paper.

title: The Bank of England targets 2% inflation
body: The Bank of England's target is to keep inflation around 2% a year. It mainly does this by changing interest rates: raising them makes borrowing pricier and cools spending, while lowering them encourages spending.

rq.prompt: What's the Bank's main tool for controlling inflation?

why: A little inflation is thought healthier than falling prices.

title: The first number sways your guess
body: In a famous 1974 study, people saw a wheel of fortune land on a number before estimating how many African countries were in the UN. Those who saw a higher number gave higher guesses. This is the anchoring effect.

why: We adjust from a starting point, but not far enough.

title: Losses hurt more than gains feel good
body: Research on loss aversion suggests losing something feels roughly twice as bad as gaining the same thing feels good. It explains why people hold onto falling shares and hate giving up things they own.

why: Avoiding losses may have helped our ancestors survive.

title: Forgetting follows a curve
body: In the 1880s Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised nonsense syllables and tested himself. He found memory drops steeply within the first day, then levels off. Reviewing at spaced intervals flattens the curve, the idea Inkling's reviews are built on.

rq.prompt: What flattens the forgetting curve?

title: Testing yourself beats re-reading
body: Many studies show that trying to recall information, even guessing wrongly, strengthens memory more than reading it again. It's called the testing effect, and it's why Inkling asks you a question before showing the answer.

q.prompt: Which helps you remember more?

title: Half of people miss the gorilla
body: In a 1999 experiment, people counted basketball passes in a video. A person in a gorilla suit walked through the scene, and about half the viewers didn't notice. Focused attention can make us blind to the unexpected.

q.prompt: What did many viewers miss in the basketball video?
options: A person in a gorilla suit

rq.prompt: What does the gorilla study show?
options: Focus can blind us to obvious things

why: This is called inattentional blindness.

title: Familiarity breeds liking
body: Psychologist Robert Zajonc found people tend to prefer things simply because they've seen them before, even nonsense words or shapes. This 'mere exposure effect' is one reason adverts repeat so often.

q.prompt: What tends to happen when we see something repeatedly?

rq.prompt: What is this effect called?

why: Familiar things feel easier to process, which feels pleasant.

title: We remember beginnings and endings
body: Given a list to remember, people best recall the first few items and the last few, while the middle blurs. This serial position effect shapes everything from shopping lists to which job candidate an interviewer remembers.

q.prompt: Which items in a list do people remember best?

rq.prompt: What is this pattern called?

why: Early items get rehearsed; late items are still fresh.

title: Onions make you cry with a gas
body: Cutting an onion breaks its cells, mixing chemicals that create a gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. When it reaches your eyes it irritates them, and they make tears to wash it away. Chilling the onion first slows the reaction.

q.prompt: Why do onions make you cry?

why: Cold slows the chemical reaction that makes the gas.

title: Chillies trick your heat sensors
body: Capsaicin, the active chemical in chillies, binds to the same nerve receptors that detect real heat. Your brain gets a 'burning' signal with no actual temperature change. Milk helps because its casein protein carries capsaicin away.

q.prompt: Does chilli actually raise the temperature in your mouth?

title: Mint tricks your cold sensors
body: Menthol in mint activates the same receptors that sense cold, called TRPM8. That's why mint feels cool even at room temperature, and why menthol is used in some cooling creams.

q.prompt: Why does mint feel cold?

why: It's the mirror image of how chilli fakes heat.

title: Popcorn pops from steam pressure
body: Each popcorn kernel holds a little water inside a tough shell. Heated to about 180 °C, the water turns to steam and the pressure builds until the shell bursts. The starchy inside puffs into foam and sets.

q.prompt: What makes popcorn pop?

rq.prompt: Why do some kernels never pop?
options: Their shells leak or they're too dry

why: No sealed water, no pressure.

title: Yeast makes bread rise
body: Yeast are tiny fungi that eat sugars in dough and give off carbon dioxide gas. Stretchy gluten traps the bubbles, so the dough rises. Baking kills the yeast and sets the bubbly structure.

q.prompt: What gas makes bread rise?

rq.prompt: What traps the gas bubbles in dough?

why: Kneading builds the gluten network.

title: Salt makes ice melt below zero
body: Salt dissolves into the thin film of water on ice and lowers the temperature at which it freezes. The salty water stays liquid at temperatures where pure water would freeze, so the ice melts. It stops working well below about −10 °C.

q.prompt: How does road salt melt ice?

rq.prompt: When does road salt become much less effective?

why: Salt gets in the way of water forming ice crystals.

title: Soap rips viruses apart
body: Soap molecules have one end that loves water and another that loves fats and oils. The fat-loving ends wedge into the oily outer layer of many viruses and germs, breaking them apart, and the water washes them away.

q.prompt: How does soap destroy many viruses?
options: It breaks their fatty outer layer

rq.prompt: What do soap molecules' two ends like?

why: Twenty seconds of scrubbing gives soap time to work.

title: Stainless steel heals itself
body: Stainless steel contains at least about 10.5% chromium. The chromium reacts with oxygen to form an invisible layer that protects the iron beneath from rust. If scratched, the layer quickly re-forms.

q.prompt: What stops stainless steel rusting?

rq.prompt: What happens if stainless steel gets scratched?

why: Chromium oxide is tough and self-repairing.

title: Metal isn't colder than wood
body: In the same room, a metal bench and a wooden one are the same temperature. Metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from your skin much faster. Your nerves sense heat loss, not temperature.

q.prompt: In the same room, a metal spoon and a wooden spoon are…

rq.prompt: Why does metal feel colder?
options: It draws heat from skin faster

why: Skin senses the rate of heat flow.

title: A vacuum flask stops heat three ways
body: A vacuum flask has two walls with a vacuum between them, so heat can't conduct or move by air currents. The walls are silvered to reflect radiated heat. James Dewar invented it in 1892 for keeping chemicals cold.

q.prompt: What's between the walls of a vacuum flask?

rq.prompt: What was the vacuum flask first invented for?

why: No matter between the walls means no conduction.

title: Old bulbs were mostly heaters
body: A traditional incandescent bulb turns only about 5% of its electricity into visible light; the rest becomes heat. LEDs make the same light using around 80 to 90% less energy.

q.prompt: How much of an old bulb's energy became light?

rq.prompt: How much less energy do LEDs typically use?

why: Incandescent bulbs glow by heating a wire white-hot.

title: Electric cars recharge when braking
body: When an electric car slows down, its motor can run in reverse as a generator, turning the car's motion back into electricity for the battery. This regenerative braking also saves wear on the brake pads.

q.prompt: What happens to an electric car's energy when it brakes?
options: Some goes back into the battery

rq.prompt: What does the motor become during regenerative braking?

why: Motors and generators are the same machine run in opposite directions.

title: Planes cruise high to save fuel
body: Airliners usually cruise around 10 to 12 km up. The air there is much thinner, so there's less drag, and jet engines run efficiently. It also puts them above most weather.

q.prompt: Why do airliners fly so high?

rq.prompt: About how high do airliners usually cruise?

why: Less air to push through means less fuel burned.

title: Plane windows are round for a reason
body: In 1954, two de Havilland Comet jets broke apart in flight. Investigators traced metal fatigue cracks to the sharp corners of a rectangular opening in the cabin roof, where stress concentrates. Rounded openings spread stress evenly, which is why airliner windows are rounded.

q.prompt: Why are airliner windows rounded?

rq.prompt: Which aircraft disasters led to round windows?

why: Repeated pressurisation stresses the cabin each flight.

title: That tiny hole in plane windows
body: Airliner windows have several layers. A tiny 'breather hole' in the middle pane lets air pressure equalise between layers, so the outer pane takes the main load. It also helps stop the window fogging up.

q.prompt: What is the tiny hole in a plane window for?

rq.prompt: Which pane takes the main pressure load?

why: The inner panes are backups.

title: Why your ears pop
body: A narrow channel called the Eustachian tube links your middle ear to the back of your throat. When outside pressure changes, swallowing or yawning opens it, letting air rush through to equalise pressure, which you feel as a pop.

q.prompt: What equalises pressure in your ears?

rq.prompt: What helps your ears pop on a plane?

why: Muscles that open the tube work when you swallow.

title: Lift safety brakes made skyscrapers possible
body: In 1854, Elisha Otis stood on a lift platform and had its only rope cut in front of a crowd in New York. His spring-loaded safety brake caught it. Safe lifts made tall buildings practical.

q.prompt: What did Elisha Otis do to show off his invention?

rq.prompt: Why did safe lifts matter?

why: Fear of falling had kept buildings short.

title: Ships float by pushing water aside
body: A steel ship floats because its hollow hull pushes aside a weight of water equal to its own weight before it sinks too far. This is Archimedes' principle. Squash the same steel into a solid lump and it would sink.

q.prompt: Why does a heavy steel ship float?

rq.prompt: Whose principle explains floating?

why: Shape matters: a hull displaces far more water than a lump.

title: Antibiotics don't work on viruses
body: Antibiotics attack features of bacteria, such as their cell walls. Viruses don't have those features, so antibiotics don't help with colds or flu. Using them unnecessarily helps bacteria evolve resistance.

q.prompt: Do antibiotics treat a common cold?

rq.prompt: What does overusing antibiotics cause?

why: Bacteria that survive the drug pass on their resistance.

title: Face unlock uses thousands of invisible dots
body: Apple's Face ID projects over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto your face and reads how they land, building a 3D map. That's why a flat photo can't fool it the way it fools simpler 2D camera systems.

q.prompt: Why can't a photo fool Face ID?

rq.prompt: What does Face ID project onto your face?

why: Depth information is hard to fake with a picture.

title: Toast often lands butter side down
body: Physicist Robert Matthews showed that a slice of toast sliding off a typical table only has time to make about half a rotation before landing. So if it starts butter side up, it tends to land butter side down.

q.prompt: Why does dropped toast often land butter side down?
options: Table height allows about half a turn

rq.prompt: What would help toast land butter side up?

why: Matthews won an Ig Nobel Prize for the study in 1996.

title: F and J have bumps for a reason
body: The small ridges on the F and J keys let touch typists find the home row without looking. Your index fingers rest there, and the other fingers fall into place along the row.

q.prompt: Why do the F and J keys have bumps?
options: To find the home row by touch

rq.prompt: Which fingers rest on F and J?

why: Touch typing relies on feel, not sight.

title: You helped digitise books
body: For years, many reCAPTCHA puzzles showed two words: one the system knew, and one scanned from an old book that computers couldn't read. By typing both, millions of people helped digitise books and newspapers.

q.prompt: What did typing reCAPTCHA words once help do?

rq.prompt: How did reCAPTCHA know you were human?
options: You typed the known word right
It checked your typing speed only

why: It turned a security check into useful work.

title: The internet runs under the sea
body: The vast majority of data travelling between continents goes through fibre-optic cables on the seabed, not satellites. Hundreds of these cables crisscross the oceans, some thinner than a garden hose.

q.prompt: How does most internet data cross oceans?

rq.prompt: What do undersea internet cables carry data with?

why: Cables carry far more data, faster and cheaper, than satellites.

title: Data travels in packets
body: When you send a photo, it's chopped into thousands of small packets. Each packet may take a different route across the internet, and your friend's device puts them back in order. Lost packets are simply re-sent.

q.prompt: How does a photo travel across the internet?

rq.prompt: What happens to a lost packet?

why: Small packets share network links efficiently.

title: Screens use only three colours
body: Every pixel on your screen is made of tiny red, green and blue parts. By mixing their brightness, a screen can create millions of colours. Look at a screen with a magnifying glass and you can see the separate dots.

q.prompt: Which three colours make every colour on your screen?

rq.prompt: How do screens make yellow?

why: Your eye has three types of colour receptors.

title: £9.99 really does feel cheaper
body: Studies show prices ending in .99 make people feel something is noticeably cheaper than the round number. We read left to right, so £9.99 registers as 'nine-something'. It's called the left-digit effect.

q.prompt: Why do shops price things at £9.99?
options: The first digit sways our sense of price

rq.prompt: What's this effect called?

why: We judge numbers quickly by their first digit.

title: Many crossing buttons once did nothing
body: In 2004, The New York Times reported that most of New York's pedestrian crossing buttons no longer worked, because the lights ran on timers. Many cities still keep some buttons only for daytime or night-time use.

q.prompt: What did a 2004 report find about New York crossing buttons?

rq.prompt: Why didn't the buttons work?

why: Computerised traffic timing replaced on-demand crossings.

title: Leap years skip some centuries
body: Earth takes about 365.2422 days to go round the Sun. Adding a leap day every four years overcorrects slightly, so century years skip it unless divisible by 400. 2000 was a leap year; 1900 wasn't, and 2100 won't be.

q.prompt: Will 2100 be a leap year?

rq.prompt: Why was 2000 a leap year?

why: The rule keeps the calendar aligned with the seasons.

title: China uses a single time zone
body: China spans about five geographical time zones but uses one official time, Beijing Time. In the far west, sunrise in winter can come after 9 a.m., and some people there unofficially use a local time two hours behind.

q.prompt: How many official time zones does China use?

rq.prompt: What happens in China's far west because of this?

why: A single zone was adopted in 1949 for national unity.

title: Germany started daylight saving
body: Germany and Austria-Hungary were the first to adopt daylight saving time nationally, in 1916, to save fuel for the war effort. Britain followed a few weeks later with British Summer Time.

q.prompt: Which country first adopted daylight saving nationally?

rq.prompt: Why was daylight saving first introduced?

why: An extra hour of evening daylight cut lighting costs.

title: A second is 9 billion vibrations
body: Since 1967, one second has been officially defined as 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation from a caesium-133 atom. Atomic clocks count these and are so precise they would drift by less than a second over millions of years.

q.prompt: What defines one official second?

rq.prompt: When was this definition adopted?

why: Atoms are more regular than Earth's slightly wobbly spin.

title: Babylon gave us 60 minutes
body: We split hours into 60 minutes and circles into 360 degrees thanks to the ancient Babylonians, who counted in base 60. Sixty divides neatly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30.

q.prompt: Why are there 60 minutes in an hour?

rq.prompt: Why is 60 a handy number?
options: It divides evenly in many ways

why: Easy division made trade and astronomy simpler.

title: Most fund managers don't beat the market
body: Each year, S&P's SPIVA reports compare active investment funds with simple index funds that track a whole market. Over 10 to 15 years, the large majority of active funds do worse than their index, partly due to higher fees.

q.prompt: Over 15 years, do most active funds beat a simple index?

rq.prompt: What's one big reason active funds lag?

why: Small yearly fees compound into large differences.

title: Bitcoin has a hard cap
body: Bitcoin's code limits the total supply to 21 million coins. New coins are released ever more slowly, halving the reward roughly every four years, with the last fractions expected around the year 2140.

q.prompt: What's the maximum number of bitcoins that can exist?

rq.prompt: How often does the new-bitcoin reward halve?

why: A fixed supply was a design choice by its creator.

title: Sleep comes in 90-minute cycles
body: A night's sleep moves through repeating cycles of lighter, deeper and dreaming (REM) sleep, each roughly 90 minutes. Deep sleep dominates early in the night, while REM periods get longer toward morning.

q.prompt: Roughly how long is one sleep cycle?

rq.prompt: When do dreaming (REM) periods get longest?

why: The brain cycles through different restorative stages.

title: Sugar doesn't make children hyper
body: Many parents believe sugar makes kids hyperactive, but controlled studies, including a 1995 analysis of many trials, found no real effect on behaviour. In one study, parents told their child had sugar rated them more hyper, even when it was a placebo.

q.prompt: Does sugar make children hyperactive?

rq.prompt: What did parents do when told their child had sugar?

why: Expectation shapes what we see.

title: Cracking knuckles won't cause arthritis
body: The pop comes from gas bubbles forming in the fluid of the joint. Doctor Donald Unger cracked the knuckles of only one hand for over 60 years and found no arthritis difference between hands. Larger studies agree.

q.prompt: Does cracking your knuckles cause arthritis?

rq.prompt: What makes the knuckle pop?

why: Unger won an Ig Nobel Prize for his one-man experiment.

title: Muscle memory lives in your brain
body: When you learn to ride a bike or type, the 'muscle memory' is stored in the brain, in areas like the cerebellum and motor cortex, not in the muscles themselves. Practice makes the brain's control of movement faster and more automatic.

q.prompt: Where is 'muscle memory' actually stored?

rq.prompt: Which brain area helps fine-tune movements?

why: Repetition strengthens the brain circuits controlling a skill.

title: Habits take about two months to form
body: A 2009 UCL study tracked people building a new daily habit. On average it took about 66 days for the behaviour to feel automatic, but individuals ranged widely from 18 to 254 days. Missing a day now and then didn't ruin progress.

q.prompt: On average, how long did a new habit take to feel automatic?

rq.prompt: Did missing one day derail habit-building?

why: Consistency over weeks matters more than perfection.

title: Multitasking is mostly switching
body: When you 'multitask' on mental tasks, your brain usually switches rapidly between them. Each switch costs time and attention, so doing two demanding things at once is often slower and more error-prone than doing them one after another.

q.prompt: What does the brain mostly do when 'multitasking'?

rq.prompt: What's the cost of switching tasks?

why: Attention can only fully focus on one demanding task.

title: Most 'taste' is really smell
body: Your tongue detects only basic tastes like sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. The rich flavours of food come mostly from smell, as aromas travel up the back of your throat. That's why food tastes bland with a blocked nose.

q.prompt: Why does food taste bland when you have a cold?
options: Your sense of smell is blocked

rq.prompt: Where do most food flavours come from?

why: Aromas reach your nose from inside your mouth.

title: Decaf isn't caffeine-free
body: Decaffeination removes most but not all caffeine. A cup of decaf coffee typically still has a few milligrams, compared with around 70 to 140 mg in a regular cup.

q.prompt: Does decaf coffee contain caffeine?

rq.prompt: About how much caffeine is in regular coffee?

why: Removing every last molecule would ruin the flavour.

title: Guinness bubbles sink
body: In a pint of Guinness, bubbles near the glass wall drift downward. Scientists showed the bubbles rise in the middle, pushing liquid up, while liquid near the walls flows down, dragging bubbles with it.

q.prompt: Which way do bubbles near the glass travel in Guinness?

rq.prompt: What drags the bubbles down?
options: Liquid flowing down near the walls

why: Rising bubbles in the centre create a circulating current.

title: Mentos make cola erupt by roughness
body: Mentos sweets are covered in microscopic pits. Dropped into fizzy drink, these give dissolved carbon dioxide countless spots to form bubbles all at once. The sudden burst of gas launches a foaming fountain.

q.prompt: Why does a Mentos make cola erupt?

rq.prompt: What gas forms the fountain?

why: Bubbles need 'nucleation sites' to start forming.

source.name: Wikipedia: Diet Coke and Mentos eruption

title: The Leaning Tower leaned from the start
body: Construction of Pisa's bell tower began in 1173, and it started to lean during building because the soft ground on one side couldn't support it. Engineers straightened its tilt slightly between 1990 and 2001 to stop it falling.

q.prompt: When did the Leaning Tower of Pisa start leaning?

rq.prompt: What caused the lean?

why: Building took nearly 200 years; long pauses let the soil settle.

title: Wind twisted the Tacoma Narrows Bridge apart
body: In 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State twisted wildly in a steady wind and collapsed. It wasn't simple resonance: the wind created self-feeding 'flutter'. Engineers now test bridge designs in wind tunnels.

q.prompt: What brought down the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?

rq.prompt: What do engineers do now because of it?

why: Aerodynamic flutter can grow until a structure fails.

title: Why we use AC electricity
body: Mains electricity is alternating current, which flips direction many times a second (50 times in the UK). AC is easy to step up to high voltages for long-distance power lines, which waste less energy, then back down for homes.

q.prompt: How many times a second does UK mains current change direction?

rq.prompt: Why is AC used for power grids?
options: Its voltage is easy to change

why: High voltage means less current and less heat lost in wires.

title: A transformer needs changing current
body: Transformers change voltage using two coils of wire around an iron core. A changing current in one coil creates a changing magnetic field, which drives current in the other. More turns in the second coil means a higher voltage.

q.prompt: What device steps electricity's voltage up or down?

rq.prompt: Why don't transformers work with steady DC?
options: They need a changing magnetic field

why: Only a changing field induces current in the second coil.

title: Fuses melt to protect you
body: A fuse contains a thin wire that melts if too much current flows, breaking the circuit before wires overheat and start a fire. Circuit breakers do the same job but can be reset with a switch.

q.prompt: What does a fuse do when too much current flows?
options: Its wire melts and breaks the circuit

rq.prompt: How is a circuit breaker different from a fuse?

why: Too much current heats wires, which can cause fires.

title: UK plugs have a fuse inside
body: British plugs are unusual in containing their own fuse, typically 3 or 13 amps. They also have a longer earth pin that opens shutters in the socket, stopping objects being pushed into the live holes.

q.prompt: What's unusual inside a UK plug?

rq.prompt: What does the longer earth pin do?

why: The design dates from post-war wiring standards in 1947.

title: Solar panels make electricity from light
body: Solar cells are made from silicon layers. When light hits them, it knocks electrons loose, and the cell's structure pushes them in one direction, creating a current. Typical home panels convert about 20% of sunlight into electricity.

q.prompt: What do most solar panels use to make electricity?

rq.prompt: About how efficient are typical home panels?

why: Light energy frees electrons that then flow as current.

title: Wind turbines turn slowly but strongly
body: Big wind turbine blades look slow, but their tips can move faster than 250 km/h. A gearbox or special generator converts the slow, powerful turning of the rotor into electricity.

q.prompt: How fast can the tips of large wind turbine blades move?

rq.prompt: Why do turbines look slow?
options: They're huge, so tips cover great distances
They really are slow at the tips
An optical illusion from the blades' colour

why: The longer the blade, the faster the tip for the same turning rate.

title: Phones know which way is up
body: Phones contain tiny accelerometers, microscopic structures that shift slightly as the phone tilts or moves. Measuring these shifts tells the phone which way gravity is pulling, so the screen can rotate.

q.prompt: How does your phone know when you rotate it?

rq.prompt: What force does the accelerometer detect when still?

why: Microscopic parts bend slightly under gravity's pull.

title: Your phone has a compass
body: Smartphones contain a magnetometer that senses Earth's magnetic field. Map apps combine it with GPS to show which way you're facing. Nearby magnets or metal can confuse it, which is why apps sometimes ask you to wave your phone in a figure of eight.

q.prompt: Why do map apps ask you to wave your phone in a figure of eight?

rq.prompt: What sensor works as a phone's compass?

why: Moving it lets the phone separate Earth's field from local interference.

title: Why the 'save' icon is a floppy disk
body: The save icon shows a 3.5-inch floppy disk, a storage format popular in the 1980s and 1990s that held 1.44 MB, less than one phone photo today. The icon stuck long after the disks disappeared.

q.prompt: What does the classic 'save' icon show?
