rq.prompt: How much could a standard 3.5-inch floppy hold?

why: Familiar symbols outlive the objects they show.

title: Wet phones: rice doesn't help much
body: Putting a wet phone in rice is popular advice, but tests suggest it works no better than leaving the phone to dry in open air. Apple's own guidance advises against rice, partly because small particles can get inside.

q.prompt: Does putting a wet phone in rice help it dry?
options: Not really, air-drying works as well

rq.prompt: What does Apple advise against for wet phones?

why: Rice absorbs little moisture from inside a sealed phone.

source.name: Apple Support: liquid-detection alert on iPhone

title: Planes' black boxes are orange
body: A plane's 'black box' flight recorders are actually painted bright orange so they're easier to find after a crash. They're built to survive huge impacts and fires, and send an underwater beacon signal.

q.prompt: What colour is an aeroplane's 'black box'?

rq.prompt: Why are flight recorders brightly coloured?

why: Visibility matters most when searching wreckage.

title: Escalators were once a ride
body: An early version of the escalator was installed as a novelty ride at Coney Island in 1896. When Harrods installed one in London in 1898, staff reportedly offered nervous customers brandy at the top.

q.prompt: What did Harrods reportedly offer customers after its first escalator?

rq.prompt: Where was an early escalator installed as a ride?

why: Moving stairs were thrilling and a little scary at first.

title: Cat's eyes on roads need no power
body: Percy Shaw invented reflective road studs in 1934 in Yorkshire, reportedly inspired by a cat's eyes shining in his headlights. Each stud's rubber casing squeezes down when a car drives over it, wiping the glass clean.

q.prompt: Who invented 'cat's eyes' road studs?

rq.prompt: How do cat's eyes stay clean?
options: Rubber wipes them as cars drive over

why: Glass beads reflect headlights straight back to the driver.

title: Traffic lights came before cars
body: The first traffic signal was installed outside London's Houses of Parliament in 1868 to control horse-drawn carriages. It was gas-lit and operated by a police officer. It exploded the next year, injuring the officer.

q.prompt: When was the first traffic signal installed?

rq.prompt: What happened to the first traffic signal?

why: A gas leak caused the explosion.

title: Supermarket music is chosen carefully
body: Studies in shops have found that slower background music can make people walk more slowly and spend more. In one wine shop study, playing French music boosted French wine sales, while German music boosted German wine.

q.prompt: What did French music do in a wine shop study?

rq.prompt: What can slow background music encourage?

why: Cues we barely notice can steer choices.

title: Ice is slippery for surprising reasons
body: Many people believe skates melt ice by pressure. The pressure effect is actually far too small. Scientists think a thin, water-like layer naturally exists on ice's surface, and friction from sliding adds more melting.

q.prompt: Is pressure melting the main reason ice is slippery?
options: No, the effect is too small

rq.prompt: What do scientists think makes ice slippery?

why: Surface molecules are less tightly bound than those inside.

title: Non-stick pans use PTFE
body: Non-stick coatings are usually PTFE, better known by the brand name Teflon, discovered by accident in 1938 by chemist Roy Plunkett. Its molecules are so slippery that almost nothing can grip them.

q.prompt: How was Teflon discovered?

rq.prompt: What is Teflon's chemical name?

why: Fluorine atoms shield its carbon backbone from sticking.

title: Coffee and tea stains form rings
body: When a spilled drop of coffee dries, the edge stays pinned while liquid evaporates fastest there. Fluid flows outward to replace it, carrying coffee particles, which pile up into a dark ring. Physicists call it the coffee ring effect.

q.prompt: Why do coffee spills dry into rings?
options: Liquid flows to the edge as it evaporates
The cup's rim leaves a mark

rq.prompt: What do physicists call this?

why: Evaporation is fastest at a drop's thin edge.

title: Fireworks colours come from metals
body: Firework colours come from metal salts that glow at particular colours when heated: strontium gives red, sodium yellow, barium green and copper blue. Blue is the hardest to make bright.

q.prompt: What makes the colours in fireworks?

rq.prompt: Which metal gives fireworks a red colour?

why: Each element gives off its own colours of light when hot.

title: Why bubbles are round
body: A soap bubble's film pulls inward like a stretched skin. A sphere is the shape that encloses a given amount of air with the least surface area, so surface tension pulls bubbles into spheres.

q.prompt: Why are bubbles spherical?
options: A sphere has the least surface for its volume

rq.prompt: What force pulls a bubble into shape?

why: Nature tends to minimise energy, and less surface means less energy.

title: Velcro, zips and buttons: the zip's story
body: Early zip-like fasteners appeared in the 1890s, but Gideon Sundback's improved design in 1913 made them reliable. The name 'zipper' came from a 1920s brand of rubber boots with zip fasteners.

q.prompt: Where does the name 'zipper' come from?

rq.prompt: Who made the zip reliable in 1913?

why: Interlocking teeth pulled together by a slider made it work.

title: Why you see stars after standing up fast
body: When you stand up quickly, gravity pulls blood toward your legs and your blood pressure briefly drops. Your brain gets slightly less blood until your body adjusts, which can cause dizziness and spots in your vision.

q.prompt: Why can standing up fast make you dizzy?

rq.prompt: What does your body do to fix it?
options: Tightens blood vessels and speeds the heart

why: It takes a few seconds for reflexes to catch up.

title: Hiccups are a diaphragm spasm
body: A hiccup is a sudden contraction of your diaphragm, followed by your vocal cords snapping shut, which makes the 'hic' sound. Common triggers include eating fast, fizzy drinks and excitement. Most bouts stop on their own within minutes.

q.prompt: What makes the 'hic' sound?

rq.prompt: Which muscle spasms in a hiccup?

why: The closing vocal cords cut off the sudden breath in.

title: Contagious yawning is real
body: Seeing, hearing or even reading about yawning can make you yawn. Studies find people are more likely to catch yawns from family and friends than from strangers, though why we yawn at all is still debated.

q.prompt: Who are you most likely to 'catch' a yawn from?

rq.prompt: Do scientists fully understand why we yawn?
options: Yes, it cools the brain only

why: Contagious yawning may be linked to social bonding.

title: Venus spins slower than it orbits
body: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once on its axis, but only about 225 days to go around the Sun. So one full rotation of Venus lasts longer than its year. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.

q.prompt: On Venus, which takes longer?

rq.prompt: About how long does Venus take to spin once?

why: 243 days to rotate beats 225 days to orbit.

title: Neutron stars are unbelievably dense
body: A neutron star packs more mass than our Sun into a ball about 20 km across. NASA says a sugar-cube-sized lump of its material would weigh around a billion tonnes on Earth.

q.prompt: A sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about…

rq.prompt: Roughly how wide is a neutron star?
options: About as wide as the Sun

why: Atoms are crushed until mostly neutrons remain, packed tight.

title: Sunlight is 8 minutes old
body: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. If the Sun vanished, we would keep seeing it, and orbiting it, for those eight minutes.

q.prompt: How old is the sunlight hitting you right now?

rq.prompt: If the Sun vanished, how long until we'd notice?

why: The Sun is about 150 million km away and light covers about 300,000 km each second.

title: Bananas are berries, strawberries aren't
body: To a botanist, a berry is a fleshy fruit grown from one flower with one ovary, usually holding several seeds. Bananas, tomatoes and grapes qualify. Strawberries don't: they grow from a flower's swollen base, and the 'seeds' outside are actually tiny fruits.

q.prompt: Which of these is a true berry, botanically?

rq.prompt: What are the 'seeds' on a strawberry's outside?

why: Berry is a botanical category based on how the fruit forms.

title: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
body: An octopus has two hearts that pump blood through the gills and a third for the rest of the body. Its blood uses a copper-based protein, haemocyanin, to carry oxygen, which turns it blue.

q.prompt: How many hearts does an octopus have?

rq.prompt: Why is octopus blood blue?

why: Haemocyanin uses copper; our haemoglobin uses iron.

title: Ice floats because water is weird
body: Most substances are denser as solids. Water expands by about 9% when it freezes, because its molecules lock into an open hexagon pattern. That's why ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down, letting fish survive underneath.

q.prompt: What happens to water's volume when it freezes?

rq.prompt: Why do lakes freeze from the top down?
options: Ice is less dense than water
The bottom is warmer from the Sun

why: Hydrogen bonds hold frozen water in a spacious crystal.

title: Saturn is less dense than water
body: Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium, giving it an average density of about 0.69 grams per cubic centimetre. Water is 1.0. It's the only planet in our solar system less dense than water.

q.prompt: Which planet is less dense than water?

rq.prompt: What is Saturn mostly made of?

why: Gas giants are huge but made of light elements.

title: Everest isn't the farthest point from Earth's centre
body: Earth bulges at the equator. Chimborazo in Ecuador is almost on the equator, so its summit is about 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's, even though Everest is far higher above sea level.

q.prompt: Which summit is farthest from Earth's centre?

rq.prompt: Why does Chimborazo stick out further?

why: Spinning makes Earth wider around the middle.

title: Sharks are older than trees
body: The earliest shark-like fossils, mainly scales, date back about 450 million years. The first true trees appeared around 385 million years ago. Sharks have outlasted several mass extinctions, including the one that ended the dinosaurs.

q.prompt: Which came first on Earth?

rq.prompt: Roughly how long ago did sharks appear?

why: Fossil sharks predate the first forests by tens of millions of years.

title: Tardigrades survived outer space
body: Tardigrades, or water bears, are animals about half a millimetre long. In 2007 some were sent into orbit and exposed to the vacuum of space. Many survived and later had healthy offspring. They do it by drying out into a dormant state.

q.prompt: Which animal survived direct exposure to space?

rq.prompt: How do tardigrades survive extremes?
options: They dry out and go dormant

why: Dormant tardigrades barely metabolise, so they're hard to damage.

title: Sealed honey keeps almost forever
body: Honey is very low in water and fairly acidic, and bees add an enzyme that produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. Microbes struggle to grow in it, so sealed honey can last for years. It may crystallise, but that doesn't mean it has spoiled.

q.prompt: What usually happens to old sealed honey?
options: It crystallises but is still fine

rq.prompt: Why do microbes struggle in honey?
options: Too little water and too acidic

why: Sugar draws water out of microbes, drying them out.

title: Babies have more bones than adults
body: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones, many made partly of cartilage. As the child grows, several fuse together, for example in the skull and the base of the spine. Adults usually end up with 206.

q.prompt: Who has more bones?

rq.prompt: How many bones does an adult usually have?

why: Separate infant bones fuse as we grow.

title: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
body: A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 °C in a split second. The visible surface of the Sun is about 5,500 °C. The sudden expansion of that superheated air is what we hear as thunder.

q.prompt: Which is hotter?

rq.prompt: What causes thunder?

why: The air in the channel is heated almost instantly and explodes outward.

title: The Moon is drifting away
body: Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon, and scientists bounce lasers off them. These measurements show the Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

q.prompt: What is the Moon doing, very slowly?

rq.prompt: How do we measure the Moon's drift?
options: Lasers bounced off mirrors left by astronauts

why: Tides transfer some of Earth's spin energy to the Moon's orbit.

title: Earth's days are getting longer
body: The Moon's tides act like a gentle brake on Earth's spin. On average, the day grows longer by roughly 2 milliseconds per century. Hundreds of millions of years ago, a day lasted only about 21 to 22 hours.

q.prompt: What's slowly happening to the length of Earth's day?

rq.prompt: What mainly slows Earth's spin?

why: Tidal friction drains a little of Earth's rotation energy.

title: Mars has a volcano 2.5 times Everest
body: Olympus Mons on Mars rises about 22 km, roughly two and a half times the height of Everest above sea level, and spreads about 600 km across. It is one of the largest volcanoes known in the solar system.

q.prompt: Where is the tallest volcano in our solar system found?

rq.prompt: About how tall is Olympus Mons?

why: Lower gravity and no moving plates let Martian volcanoes grow huge.

title: A million Earths fit inside the Sun
body: The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth. Because volume grows with the cube of width, you could fit roughly 1.3 million Earths inside it. The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system.

q.prompt: Roughly how many Earths could fit inside the Sun?

rq.prompt: What share of the solar system's mass is in the Sun?

why: 109 times wider means about 109³ ≈ 1.3 million times the volume.

title: Space is silent
body: Sound is a vibration passing through matter, like air or water. Space is a near-perfect vacuum, so there's almost nothing to carry it. Astronauts talk by radio, which uses light-speed electromagnetic waves that don't need air.

q.prompt: Could you hear an explosion in space?
options: No, there's nothing to carry sound

rq.prompt: Why can radio work in space when sound can't?
options: Radio waves don't need matter to travel

why: Sound needs molecules to bump into each other.

title: The coldest known place is a nebula
body: The Boomerang Nebula, about 5,000 light-years away, sits at about 1 degree above absolute zero. That's colder than the faint afterglow of the Big Bang that fills space. Gas rushing out of a dying star cools as it expands.

q.prompt: Where is the coldest natural place known in the universe?

rq.prompt: How does the Boomerang Nebula get so cold?
options: Gas cools as it rapidly expands

why: Rapidly expanding gas cools, like spray from an aerosol can.

title: Wombats poo cubes
body: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, the only animal known to do so. A 2018 study found the last part of their intestine stretches unevenly, with stiffer and stretchier sections that shape the poo into cubes. Wombats use the piles to mark territory.

q.prompt: Which animal produces cube-shaped poo?

rq.prompt: What shapes wombat poo into cubes?

why: Different parts of the gut wall stretch differently.

title: Crows remember faces
body: In a University of Washington study, researchers wore a particular mask while trapping crows. For years afterwards, crows scolded anyone wearing that mask, including birds that were never trapped. They seemed to learn the face from others.

q.prompt: What did crows do years after seeing a 'dangerous' mask?

rq.prompt: How did untrapped crows learn to fear the mask?

why: Crows have excellent memory and share warnings socially.

title: The platypus breaks the rules
body: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs. Males have venomous spurs on their back legs. It hunts underwater with its eyes, ears and nose shut, sensing the tiny electric fields of prey through its bill.

q.prompt: How does a platypus find food underwater?

rq.prompt: Which of these is true of the platypus?
options: It's a mammal that lays eggs

why: Its bill has thousands of electroreceptors.

title: Hummingbirds can fly backwards
body: Hummingbirds can twist their wings in a figure-eight pattern, getting lift on both the forward and back strokes. That lets them hover in place and fly backwards. No other bird sustains backward flight like that.

q.prompt: Which bird can fly backwards?

rq.prompt: What lets hummingbirds hover?

why: Their shoulder joint lets the wing rotate almost fully.

title: Old windows aren't melting
body: A popular myth says glass is a slow liquid, so old windows are thicker at the bottom. In fact, early glassmaking produced uneven panes and builders often set the thick edge downward. At room temperature glass would need far longer than the universe's age to flow visibly.

q.prompt: Why are some old window panes thicker at the bottom?
options: They were made uneven and fitted that way

rq.prompt: At room temperature, does glass flow visibly over centuries?

why: Glass is an amorphous solid with no measurable flow at room temperature.

title: Diamond and pencil lead are the same element
body: Diamond and graphite, the 'lead' in pencils, are both pure carbon. In diamond each atom bonds tightly to four neighbours in a rigid 3D network. In graphite, atoms form flat sheets that slide over each other, leaving marks on paper.

q.prompt: What do diamonds and pencil 'lead' have in common?

rq.prompt: Why does graphite leave marks on paper?
options: Its sheets of atoms slide off

why: Same atoms, different arrangement, very different properties.

title: Atoms are almost entirely empty
body: An atom's nucleus is roughly 100,000 times smaller across than the atom itself. If a nucleus were a pea in the centre of a football stadium, the electrons would be buzzing around the outer stands. Nearly all the mass sits in that tiny centre.

q.prompt: Most of an atom is…

rq.prompt: Where is nearly all of an atom's mass?

why: Electrons are tiny and spread out; protons and neutrons are heavy and central.

title: Earth's core is as hot as the Sun's surface
body: Earth's inner core is a solid ball of iron and nickel at roughly 5,200 °C, close to the temperature of the Sun's visible surface. It stays solid despite the heat because the pressure down there is immense.

q.prompt: Earth's inner core is about as hot as…

rq.prompt: Why is the inner core solid despite the heat?

why: Pressure raises the melting point of iron.

title: Venus is hotter than Mercury
body: Mercury is closest to the Sun, but Venus is the hottest planet. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, keeping the surface around 465 °C, hot enough to melt lead, day and night.

q.prompt: Which is the hottest planet?

rq.prompt: What makes Venus so hot?
options: A thick CO₂ atmosphere trapping heat

why: Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its heat escapes.

title: Pluto hasn't finished a lap since we found it
body: Pluto was discovered in 1930. It takes about 248 Earth years to orbit the Sun, so it won't complete its first full orbit since discovery until around 2178.

q.prompt: Has Pluto completed an orbit since its discovery in 1930?

rq.prompt: How long is a year on Pluto?

why: Far-away planets move slowly on very long paths.

title: Moon footprints could last ages
body: The Moon has no wind or rain to wear away the footprints left by Apollo astronauts. Only tiny meteorite impacts and solar radiation slowly disturb the dust, so the prints could survive for millions of years.

q.prompt: Why do Apollo footprints survive on the Moon?
options: The dust is glued by ice

rq.prompt: What slowly erodes lunar footprints?

why: Without weather, very little moves the surface.

title: Jupiter's storm is bigger than Earth
body: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm wider than Earth. It has been watched continuously since at least the 1830s, though it has been shrinking. Its winds reach several hundred kilometres an hour.

q.prompt: How big is Jupiter's Great Red Spot?
options: About the size of the UK

rq.prompt: What is the Great Red Spot?

why: Jupiter has no solid surface to slow storms down.

title: Trillions of neutrinos pass through you
body: Neutrinos are ghostly particles made in huge numbers by the Sun's nuclear reactions. Trillions pass through your body every second, day and night, because they rarely interact with anything. They even go straight through the whole Earth.

q.prompt: How many neutrinos pass through your body each second?

rq.prompt: Why don't we notice neutrinos?
options: They almost never interact with matter

why: Neutrinos have no charge and almost no mass.

title: Ocean plankton make much of our oxygen
body: Tiny ocean plants and algae called phytoplankton photosynthesise just like trees. Scientists estimate that the ocean produces around half of Earth's oxygen, much of it by phytoplankton too small to see.

q.prompt: Roughly how much of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean?

rq.prompt: What makes most ocean oxygen?

why: Phytoplankton are vast in number and photosynthesise fast.

title: Rats laugh when tickled
body: Neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp found that rats make high-pitched chirps when tickled, too high for humans to hear. They chase the tickling hand for more. He argued the chirps are a simple form of laughter.

q.prompt: What do rats do when tickled?

rq.prompt: Why can't we hear rat laughter?

why: The chirps are around 50 kHz, above human hearing.

title: There are about 20 quadrillion ants
body: A 2022 study estimated about 20 quadrillion ants live on Earth, that's 20,000,000,000,000,000. Together they weigh more than all wild birds and wild mammals combined.

q.prompt: Roughly how many ants are on Earth?

rq.prompt: Ants together weigh more than…
options: All wild birds and mammals combined

why: Ants live almost everywhere on land in huge colonies.

source.name: PNAS: The global population of ants (2022)

title: Butterflies taste with their feet
body: Butterflies have taste sensors on their feet. When they land on a leaf, they can tell if it's the right plant to lay eggs on just by standing on it. Their caterpillars will need to eat that plant.

q.prompt: What do butterflies taste with?

rq.prompt: Why do female butterflies 'taste' leaves?
options: To pick plants for their eggs

why: Chemoreceptors on the legs detect plant chemicals.

title: Your blood is never blue
body: Veins look blue through skin, but the blood inside is always red. It's darker red when low in oxygen. Skin absorbs red light more than blue, and how light scatters makes veins look bluish.

q.prompt: What colour is the blood in your veins?

rq.prompt: Why do veins look blue?
options: How skin absorbs and scatters light

why: Haemoglobin is red with or without oxygen.

title: You have more than five senses
body: Beyond sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, you sense balance, the position of your limbs, temperature, pain and even how full your bladder is. Scientists count anywhere from about 9 to over 20 senses, depending on how they're defined.

q.prompt: How many senses do humans have?

rq.prompt: Which is a real sense beyond the classic five?

why: Proprioception tells you where your hand is with your eyes closed.

title: The tongue map is a myth
body: Diagrams once showed the tongue split into zones for sweet, salty, sour and bitter. That came from a misread early-1900s study. In reality, taste buds all over the tongue can detect every basic taste.

q.prompt: Is the tip of your tongue the only place that tastes sweet?
options: No, all areas taste all tastes

rq.prompt: Where did the tongue map come from?

why: Receptors for each taste are spread across the tongue.

title: Antarctica is the biggest desert
body: A desert is defined by low precipitation, not heat. Inland Antarctica gets about as little as the Sahara, so it counts as a desert, and at around 14 million km² it's the largest on Earth.

q.prompt: What is the world's largest desert?

rq.prompt: What makes somewhere a desert?

why: Cold air holds little moisture, so polar regions get little snow.

title: Light could circle Earth 7 times a second
body: Light travels at almost 300,000 km per second. Earth's circumference is about 40,000 km, so in one second a beam could, in theory, go around the planet about seven and a half times.

q.prompt: How many times could light circle Earth in one second?

rq.prompt: Roughly how fast is light?

title: A year on Mercury is 88 days
body: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and moves fastest. It completes an orbit in just 88 Earth days. Because it spins slowly, one sunrise to the next on Mercury lasts about 176 Earth days, two of its years.

q.prompt: How long is a year on Mercury?

rq.prompt: On Mercury, sunrise to sunrise lasts about…

why: Orbit is fast, spin is slow, so its solar day is very long.

title: Sunsets on Mars are blue
body: On Earth, sunsets glow orange-red. On Mars, fine dust in the air scatters blue light forward, close to the direction of the Sun. NASA rovers have photographed cool blue glows around the setting Sun.

q.prompt: What colour are sunsets on Mars?

rq.prompt: What causes blue Martian sunsets?

why: Martian dust particles are just the right size to send blue light forward.

title: More trees on Earth than stars in our galaxy
body: A 2015 study estimated that Earth has about 3 trillion trees. The Milky Way has somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars. So trees outnumber our galaxy's stars by several times.

q.prompt: Which is more numerous?

rq.prompt: About how many trees are on Earth?

why: Satellite data plus ground counts gave the 3-trillion estimate.

title: Each of your cells holds 2 metres of DNA
body: If you uncoiled the DNA in a single human cell and laid it end to end, it would stretch about 2 metres. It fits inside a nucleus far smaller than a pinhead by wrapping around proteins and folding tightly.

q.prompt: How long is the DNA in one of your cells, stretched out?

rq.prompt: How does all that DNA fit in a cell?
options: Most of it is outside the cell

why: DNA coils around histone proteins, then coils again.

title: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day
body: At around 70 beats a minute, your heart beats roughly 100,000 times every day. Over a lifetime that's billions of beats, without ever taking a rest.

q.prompt: About how many times does your heart beat each day?

rq.prompt: A typical resting heart rate is about…

title: Red blood cells have no nucleus
body: Human red blood cells push out their nucleus as they mature. That leaves more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen and lets them bend through tiny capillaries. Without a nucleus they can't repair themselves, so each lasts about 120 days.

q.prompt: What do human red blood cells lack?

rq.prompt: How long does a red blood cell usually last?

why: Dropping the nucleus frees space for oxygen carriers.

title: Helium was found in the Sun first
body: In 1868 astronomers studying sunlight during an eclipse spotted a mysterious yellow line in its spectrum. It belonged to an unknown element, named helium after Helios, the Greek Sun god. It wasn't found on Earth until 1895.

q.prompt: Where was helium first discovered?

rq.prompt: What is helium named after?

why: Each element leaves a unique fingerprint of lines in light.

title: Most of the universe is invisible
body: Ordinary matter, everything made of atoms, is only about 5% of the universe. About 27% is dark matter, which we detect only by its gravity. The remaining 68% is dark energy, which seems to be speeding up the universe's expansion.

q.prompt: What share of the universe is ordinary matter like stars and us?

rq.prompt: What makes up the biggest share of the universe?

why: Galaxy motions and the cosmic background reveal what we can't see.

title: Voyager 1 is in interstellar space
body: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in 2012, the first human-made object to do so. It is now over 24 billion km away, and its radio signals take around a day to reach us.

q.prompt: What is the farthest human-made object?

rq.prompt: When did Voyager 1 enter interstellar space?

why: It's been flying outward at about 17 km per second for decades.

title: The space station sees 16 sunrises a day
body: The International Space Station orbits about 400 km up at roughly 28,000 km/h. It circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so astronauts on board see around 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.

q.prompt: How many sunrises do ISS astronauts see each day?

rq.prompt: How long does one ISS orbit take?

why: 24 hours ÷ 90 minutes ≈ 16 orbits.

title: Astronauts grow taller in space
body: Without gravity squashing the spine, the discs between vertebrae spread out. Astronauts can grow up to about 3% taller in orbit, often a few centimetres. They shrink back within months of returning to Earth.

q.prompt: What happens to astronauts' height in space?

rq.prompt: Why do astronauts grow in orbit?

why: Gravity normally compresses your spine slightly every day.

source.name: Wikipedia: Effect of spaceflight on the human body

title: Fingernails outpace toenails
body: Fingernails grow about 3.5 mm a month, roughly two to three times faster than toenails. A whole fingernail regrows in around six months; a big toenail can take over a year.

q.prompt: Which grow faster?

rq.prompt: How long does a fingernail take to fully regrow?

why: Nail growth links to blood flow and use, both higher in fingers.

title: Giraffes have seven neck bones, like you
body: Despite their huge necks, giraffes have the same number of neck vertebrae as humans and most mammals: seven. Each giraffe neck bone can be over 25 cm long.

q.prompt: How many neck vertebrae does a giraffe have?

rq.prompt: How does a giraffe's neck get so long?
options: Each of the seven bones is very long

why: Almost all mammals share the seven-vertebra plan.

title: Elephants can't jump
body: Adult elephants can't jump. Their bones point straight down to support their weight, and their ankles lack the springiness needed. Even when moving fast, an elephant keeps at least one foot on the ground.

q.prompt: Can an adult elephant jump?

rq.prompt: When moving fast, an elephant always keeps…

why: Pillar-like legs suit carrying weight, not springing.

title: Cheetahs purr but can't roar
body: Big cats split into two groups. Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars can roar thanks to a stretchy throat structure. Cheetahs have a rigid one, like house cats, so they purr, chirp and meow instead.

q.prompt: Which sound can a cheetah make?

rq.prompt: What lets lions roar but not cheetahs?

why: The roaring cats have a flexible, partly ossified hyoid.

title: Flamingos are pink because of food
body: Flamingos aren't born pink. Their colour comes from pigments called carotenoids in the algae and tiny shrimp they eat. Flamingos in zoos are fed supplements, or they fade toward white.

q.prompt: Why are flamingos pink?

rq.prompt: What colour are flamingo chicks?

why: Carotenoids are the same pigments that make carrots orange.

title: Starfish have no brain and no blood
body: Sea stars have no brain, instead using a ring of nerves around their mouth. They also have no blood: they pump seawater through a network of canals to move their tiny tube feet.

q.prompt: What does a starfish lack?

rq.prompt: What do sea stars pump through their bodies?

why: The water vascular system replaces blood for movement.

title: A jellyfish that can turn back time
body: When stressed or injured, the 'immortal jellyfish' Turritopsis dohrnii can turn its adult body back into a young polyp and start its life cycle again. It can still be eaten or get sick, but it can, in theory, avoid dying of old age.

q.prompt: What can the 'immortal jellyfish' do?
options: Regrow from one cell in a day

rq.prompt: Can the immortal jellyfish still die?

why: Its cells can transform into other cell types.

title: Mantis shrimp punch like bullets
body: Peacock mantis shrimp swing a club-like limb at about 80 km/h, with acceleration similar to a small-calibre bullet. The strike is so fast it creates bubbles that collapse with a second blow of heat and light. They smash crab shells open.

q.prompt: What's special about a mantis shrimp's strike?
options: One of the fastest punches in nature

rq.prompt: What extra force does the strike create?
options: A sound wave that stuns fish

why: The limb is spring-loaded and released like a catapult.

title: Bees dance directions
body: A honeybee that finds food returns to the hive and performs a 'waggle dance'. The angle of the dance relative to straight up tells others the direction relative to the Sun, and the length of the waggle tells the distance.

q.prompt: How do honeybees tell each other where food is?

rq.prompt: In the waggle dance, what does waggle length show?

why: Karl von Frisch decoded the dance and won a Nobel Prize in 1973.

title: Owls turn their heads 270 degrees
body: An owl's eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in their sockets, so it can't roll them. Instead it can rotate its head up to about 270 degrees. Extra neck vertebrae and special blood vessels keep blood flowing while it twists.

q.prompt: Why do owls turn their heads so far?

rq.prompt: About how far can an owl turn its head?

why: Owl eyes are tubular, giving big pupils but no movement.

title: Electric eels can zap 860 volts
body: In 2019 scientists described a new electric eel species, Electrophorus voltai, which can discharge up to 860 volts, the strongest known from any animal. A UK mains socket supplies 230 volts. Electric eels are actually knifefish, not true eels.

q.prompt: What's the strongest shock recorded from an animal?

rq.prompt: What are electric eels, really?

why: Thousands of special cells stack up like batteries.

title: Some bamboo grows nearly a metre a day
body: Certain bamboo species can grow up to about 90 cm in a single day, among the fastest growth of any plant. Bamboo is technically a giant grass, and a new shoot can reach full height in just a few months.

q.prompt: Bamboo is a type of…

rq.prompt: How fast can some bamboo grow?
options: Up to about 90 cm a day

why: Each segment stretches at once rather than growing from the tip.

title: The smell of rain has a name
body: That earthy smell after rain is called petrichor. Much of it comes from geosmin, a chemical made by soil bacteria. Human noses are extraordinarily sensitive to geosmin, detecting it at concentrations of just a few parts per trillion.

q.prompt: What makes the earthy smell after rain?

rq.prompt: What is the smell after rain called?

why: Raindrops kick geosmin and plant oils into the air.

title: Magnetic north is on the move
body: The north magnetic pole, where compasses point, wanders as Earth's molten iron core churns. In the early 2000s it was drifting about 50 km a year, from Canada toward Siberia. Maps and phone navigation are updated to keep up.

q.prompt: Does magnetic north stay in one place?

rq.prompt: What makes the magnetic pole move?
options: Churning liquid iron in Earth's core

why: Earth's magnetic field comes from flowing metal deep inside.

title: Earth's magnetic field flips
body: Rocks record that Earth's magnetic north and south have swapped many times. The last full reversal happened about 780,000 years ago. Reversals take hundreds to thousands of years and don't follow a regular schedule.

q.prompt: Have Earth's magnetic poles ever swapped?

rq.prompt: When was the last full magnetic reversal?

why: Magnetic minerals in cooling lava lock in the field's direction.

title: Seasons come from tilt, not distance
body: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter. Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees, so each hemisphere takes turns getting more direct sunlight and longer days.

q.prompt: Why is it warmer in summer?
options: Earth's tilt gives more direct sunlight
Earth is closer to the Sun

rq.prompt: When is Earth closest to the Sun?

why: Direct light concentrates more energy on each patch of ground.

title: The Moon has quakes
body: Seismometers left by Apollo astronauts recorded thousands of moonquakes. Some come from deep inside, some from meteorite hits, and some from the surface warming after the long lunar night. Shallow moonquakes can rumble on for many minutes.

q.prompt: Does the Moon have earthquakes?

rq.prompt: How do we know about moonquakes?

why: Earth's tides stretch the Moon, and its surface expands and contracts with heat.

title: The 'dark side' of the Moon isn't dark
body: The Moon always shows us the same face, so the other half is called the far side. It gets just as much sunlight as the near side. During a new Moon, when we see no light, the far side is fully lit.

q.prompt: Does the far side of the Moon get sunlight?
options: Yes, as much as the near side

rq.prompt: Why do we only see one side of the Moon?

why: 'Dark' meant unknown, not unlit.

source.name: Wikipedia: Far side of the Moon

title: Most shooting stars are tiny
body: A shooting star, or meteor, is usually a speck of space dust no bigger than a grain of sand. It hits the atmosphere at tens of kilometres per second and burns up about 100 km above the ground, glowing as it goes.

q.prompt: How big is a typical shooting star?

rq.prompt: Why do meteors glow?
options: They heat up hitting the air at huge speed

why: Speed, not size, makes the light show.

title: You can see 2.5-million-year-old light
body: On a dark night, the Andromeda Galaxy is a faint smudge visible without a telescope. It's about 2.5 million light-years away, so the light reaching your eye left when early human ancestors walked Earth.

q.prompt: What's the most distant thing you can see without a telescope?

rq.prompt: How long ago did Andromeda's light leave it?

why: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year.

title: Sound is faster underwater
body: Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air, but around 1,480 metres per second in water, roughly four times faster. Water molecules are packed closer, so vibrations pass along more quickly.

q.prompt: Where does sound travel faster?

rq.prompt: About how much faster is sound in water than air?

why: Denser, stiffer materials carry vibrations faster.

title: Bats aren't blind
body: 'Blind as a bat' is a myth. All bats can see, and many fruit bats have excellent eyesight and don't echolocate at all. Echolocating bats use both their eyes and their ears.

q.prompt: Are bats blind?

rq.prompt: Which bats often rely mostly on eyesight?

why: Echolocation adds to vision; it doesn't replace it.

title: Emperor penguins dive over 500 metres
body: Emperor penguins are the deepest-diving birds. They've been recorded diving more than 500 metres and holding their breath for over 20 minutes while hunting fish and squid.

q.prompt: Which bird dives the deepest?

rq.prompt: How long can emperor penguins hold their breath?

why: They slow their heart and store oxygen in muscles.

title: Arctic terns chase endless summer
body: Arctic terns fly from Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctica and back each year, a round trip averaging about 70,000 km. Over a 30-year life that adds up to roughly the distance to the Moon and back three times. They see more daylight than any other animal.

q.prompt: Which animal has the longest yearly migration?

rq.prompt: About how far does an Arctic tern fly each year?

why: Summer at both poles means near-constant daylight.

title: Axolotls regrow body parts
body: The axolotl, a Mexican salamander, can regrow lost limbs, parts of its spinal cord and heart, and even parts of its brain, without scarring. Scientists study it hoping to learn how to help human tissue heal.

q.prompt: What can an axolotl regrow?
options: Legs and parts of its heart

rq.prompt: What kind of animal is an axolotl?

why: Its cells can return to a flexible state and rebuild tissue.

title: Your brain is an energy hog
body: The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses around 20% of your resting energy. Much of that powers the constant electrical signalling between about 86 billion neurons, even while you sleep.

q.prompt: How much of your resting energy does your brain use?

rq.prompt: About how many neurons are in a human brain?

why: Keeping neurons ready to fire is energetically expensive.

title: You use far more than 10% of your brain
body: The idea that we use only 10% of our brains is a myth. Brain scans show activity across nearly all regions over a day, and damage to almost any area causes some loss of function.

q.prompt: How much of your brain do you use?

rq.prompt: What evidence busts the 10% myth?
options: Scans show activity in nearly every region

why: Different tasks use different areas, but all are used.

source.name: Wikipedia: Ten percent of the brain myth

title: Caffeine hides your tiredness
body: While you're awake, a chemical called adenosine builds up in your brain, making you feel sleepy. Caffeine has a similar shape and blocks adenosine's receptors, so the 'tired' signal can't get through. The adenosine is still there when caffeine wears off.

q.prompt: How does caffeine keep you awake?

rq.prompt: What chemical makes you feel sleepy as the day goes on?

why: Caffeine is a molecular look-alike that jams the receptor.

title: Goosebumps are a leftover
body: Tiny muscles at each hair follicle contract when you're cold or scared, making hairs stand up. In furry animals this traps warm air or makes them look bigger. For mostly hairless humans, the reflex remains but does little.

q.prompt: What were goosebumps originally for?

rq.prompt: What causes goosebumps?

why: It's a reflex inherited from hairier ancestors.

title: Air is mostly nitrogen
body: The air you breathe is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. Most of the remaining 1% is argon. Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04%, yet it has a big effect on Earth's temperature.

q.prompt: What is most of the air made of?

rq.prompt: What is the third most common gas in air?

why: Nitrogen is very unreactive, so it builds up in the air.

title: A fluffy cloud weighs hundreds of tonnes
body: The US Geological Survey estimates that a typical cumulus cloud holds about 500 tonnes of water, roughly the weight of 100 elephants. It floats because the water is spread out as tiny droplets in rising, slightly warmer air.

q.prompt: Roughly how much water is in a typical fluffy cloud?

rq.prompt: Why do clouds float?
options: Tiny droplets held up by rising air

why: Each droplet is so small it falls incredibly slowly.

source.name: USGS: How much does a cloud weigh?

title: Rainbows are really circles
body: Every rainbow is part of a full circle centred on the point opposite the Sun. From the ground, the horizon cuts off the bottom half. From a plane or a mountaintop you can sometimes see the whole ring.

q.prompt: What shape is a full rainbow?

rq.prompt: Why do we usually see only an arch?
options: The ground blocks the lower half

why: Raindrops bend light back at about 42° from the anti-solar point.

title: Snow is made of clear ice
body: Each snow crystal is made of transparent ice. Snow looks white because light bounces off the countless crystal surfaces in every direction, scattering all colours equally, which our eyes see as white.

q.prompt: What colour is ice in a snowflake?

rq.prompt: Why does snow look white?
options: Light scatters off many crystal faces

why: Scattering every colour equally makes white.

title: Everest would sink in the Mariana Trench
body: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is about 10,900 metres below sea level. Mount Everest is about 8,850 metres tall. Drop Everest in and its peak would still be about 2 km underwater.

q.prompt: If Everest were in the deepest ocean trench, would its peak stick out?
options: No, it'd be about 2 km under

rq.prompt: About how deep is Challenger Deep?

why: The trench forms where one tectonic plate dives under another.

title: Continents move as fast as nails grow
body: Tectonic plates creep a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. The Atlantic Ocean widens by roughly 2.5 cm each year as North America and Europe drift apart.

q.prompt: How fast do continents move?
options: About as fast as fingernails grow

rq.prompt: What's happening to the Atlantic Ocean?

why: Hot rock rising along the mid-Atlantic ridge pushes plates apart.

title: T. rex is closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus
body: Stegosaurus lived around 150 million years ago. Tyrannosaurus rex lived about 68 to 66 million years ago. That means less time separates T. rex from your phone than separates it from Stegosaurus.

q.prompt: Who lived closer in time to T. rex?

rq.prompt: About when did Stegosaurus live?

why: The age of dinosaurs lasted over 160 million years.

title: Birds are living dinosaurs
body: Birds evolved from small feathered dinosaurs related to Velociraptor. Scientists classify them as dinosaurs, so dinosaurs didn't all die out 66 million years ago. About 11,000 species are alive today.

q.prompt: Which animals are living dinosaurs?

rq.prompt: Which group did birds evolve from?

why: Fossils show feathers, wishbones and hollow bones in many dinosaurs.

title: Octopus arms do their own thinking
body: An octopus has about 500 million neurons, and around two-thirds of them are in its arms, not its brain. Each arm can taste, touch and react on its own, while the brain sets the overall goal.

q.prompt: Where are most of an octopus's neurons?

rq.prompt: What can a single octopus arm do by itself?

why: Spreading control out lets eight flexible arms move independently.

title: Crows make hooked tools
body: New Caledonian crows shape twigs and leaves into hooked tools to fish grubs out of logs. In a famous 2002 experiment, a crow named Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift a food basket from a tube.

q.prompt: What did Betty the crow do?
options: Opened a locked door with a key

rq.prompt: What do New Caledonian crows make in the wild?

why: Few animals besides humans make tools to a design.

title: Dolphins sleep with half a brain
body: Dolphins must surface to breathe, so they can't fully switch off. They rest one half of the brain at a time while the other stays alert, keeping one eye open to watch for danger and remember to breathe.

q.prompt: How do dolphins sleep?
options: Half their brain at a time

rq.prompt: Why can't dolphins sleep fully?

why: Breathing is a conscious action for dolphins.

title: Cats can't taste sugar
body: Cats carry a broken version of a gene needed for the sweet taste receptor, so they can't detect sweetness. It makes sense for strict meat-eaters, which rarely meet sugar. Many other carnivores, like sea lions, lost the sweet taste too.

q.prompt: Which taste can't cats detect?

rq.prompt: Why did cats lose their sweet taste?
options: As meat-eaters they didn't need it

why: Unused genes can break over evolution without harm.

title: Dogs have 50 times our smell receptors
body: Humans have about 6 million smell receptors in the nose. Dogs have up to around 300 million, and a large part of a dog's brain is devoted to analysing smells. That's why dogs can detect drugs, explosives and even some illnesses.

q.prompt: How many smell receptors can a dog have?

rq.prompt: About how many smell receptors do humans have?

why: More receptors and more brain power mean much finer sniffing.

title: The universe is 13.8 billion years old
body: By measuring the faint afterglow of the Big Bang and how fast galaxies are moving apart, astronomers estimate the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. Earth formed much later, about 4.5 billion years ago.

q.prompt: How old is the universe?

rq.prompt: How old is Earth?

why: The cosmic microwave background is light from 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

title: Hydrogen is most of everything
body: About three-quarters of all ordinary matter in the universe, by mass, is hydrogen, the simplest element. Most of the rest is helium. Every heavier element, including the carbon and oxygen in you, was made inside stars.

q.prompt: What's the most common element in the universe?

rq.prompt: Where were the carbon and oxygen in your body made?

why: The Big Bang made mostly hydrogen and helium; stars forge the rest.

source.name: Wikipedia: Abundance of the chemical elements

title: Koalas have fingerprints like ours
body: Koalas have fingerprints so similar to human ones that even under a microscope they're hard to tell apart. They evolved separately from ours, probably to help koalas grip branches and judge which leaves to eat.

q.prompt: Which animal has fingerprints very like humans'?

rq.prompt: Did koala fingerprints come from a shared ancestor with us?

why: Similar needs, like gripping, can produce similar features.

title: Pluto has a giant heart
body: When NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015, it revealed a huge bright heart-shaped region. The left half is a vast plain of nitrogen ice, about 1,000 km across, that slowly churns like a lava lamp.

q.prompt: What shape did New Horizons find on Pluto?

rq.prompt: What is Pluto's heart's left half made of?

why: Pluto is cold enough for nitrogen to freeze solid.

title: Bees see ultraviolet, not red
body: Bees can't see red well, but they see ultraviolet light. Many flowers have UV patterns, invisible to us, that act like landing strips guiding bees to the nectar.

q.prompt: Which light can bees see that we can't?

rq.prompt: What colour do bees struggle to see?

why: Bee eyes have UV, blue and green receptors.

title: Your stomach relines itself every few days
body: Your stomach acid is strong enough to break down food, so its lining needs protection. It is coated in mucus, and the surface cells are replaced every few days to keep it from digesting itself.

q.prompt: How does your stomach avoid digesting itself?

rq.prompt: How often are the stomach's surface cells replaced?

why: Constant renewal keeps damage from building up.

title: Ketchup started as fish sauce
body: The word ketchup probably comes from kê-tsiap, a fermented fish sauce from southern China. British traders brought the idea home in the 1700s, and ketchups were made from mushrooms, walnuts or oysters before tomato won out.

q.prompt: What was the original 'ketchup'?

rq.prompt: Which ingredient was NOT an early British ketchup?

why: Tomato ketchup only became standard in the 1800s.

title: Robot means forced labour
body: The word robot comes from the Czech robota, meaning forced labour. It was introduced in Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R., about artificial workers who rebel. Čapek credited his brother Josef with suggesting it.

q.prompt: What does the Czech word behind 'robot' mean?

rq.prompt: Where did 'robot' first appear?

why: The play imagined manufactured workers.

title: Muscle means little mouse
body: Muscle comes from the Latin musculus, meaning little mouse. Romans thought a flexing muscle, such as the biceps, looked like a small mouse moving under the skin.

q.prompt: What does the Latin root of 'muscle' mean?

rq.prompt: Why did Romans make that comparison?
options: Flexing muscles look like a mouse moving

why: A rippling biceps does look a bit like a mouse under a blanket.

title: Nice used to be an insult
body: Nice comes from the Latin nescius, meaning ignorant. In Middle English it meant foolish or silly. Over centuries it shifted to mean fussy, then precise, then pleasant, its main meaning today.

q.prompt: What did 'nice' originally mean in English?

rq.prompt: Which Latin word is 'nice' from?

why: Word meanings can drift far over time.

title: Silly once meant blessed
body: In Old English, sælig meant happy, fortunate or blessed. Over the centuries it drifted to innocent, then pitiable, then foolish, giving us silly.

q.prompt: What did the ancestor of 'silly' mean?

rq.prompt: Which German word shares silly's old meaning?

why: German selig kept the original 'blessed' sense.

title: A clue was a ball of thread
body: A clew was a ball of yarn. In the Greek myth, Theseus unrolled one to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth. So a 'clue' came to mean anything that helps you find your way to an answer.

q.prompt: What was a 'clew' originally?

rq.prompt: Who used one to escape a labyrinth?

why: Following the thread led to the solution.

title: Disaster means bad star
body: Disaster comes from the Italian disastro, from dis- (bad) and astro (star). It reflects an old belief that catastrophes happened when the stars and planets were badly aligned.

q.prompt: What does 'disaster' literally mean?

rq.prompt: Which old belief is behind 'disaster'?

why: Astrology shaped everyday vocabulary.

title: Quarantine means forty days
body: During plague outbreaks in the 1300s and 1400s, Venice made arriving ships wait 40 days before anyone could land. The Venetian quaranta giorni, forty days, gave us quarantine.

q.prompt: What number is hidden in 'quarantine'?

rq.prompt: Which city's plague rules gave us 'quarantine'?

why: Waiting let any hidden illness show itself.

title: Sabotage and the clog myth
body: Sabotage comes from the French saboter, linked to sabot, a wooden clog. The popular tale that workers threw clogs into machines is probably a myth; saboter meant to clatter about clumsily or to bungle a job.

q.prompt: Did 'sabotage' come from workers throwing clogs in machines?

rq.prompt: What is a 'sabot'?

why: Neat origin stories are often invented later.

title: OK began as a joke
body: In 1839, Boston newspapers had a fad for jokey abbreviations of misspellings. OK stood for 'oll korrect', a deliberate misspelling of 'all correct'. It survived thanks to an 1840 presidential campaign and the telegraph.

q.prompt: What did OK originally stand for?

rq.prompt: When did OK first appear in print?

why: Martin Van Buren's 'Old Kinderhook' campaign spread it further.

title: Goodbye means God be with you
body: Goodbye is a shortened form of 'God be with ye', common in the 1500s. Over time it was squeezed down, and 'God' changed to 'good' under the influence of greetings like 'good day'.

q.prompt: What phrase did 'goodbye' come from?

rq.prompt: Why did 'God' turn into 'good'?

why: Frequently used phrases get worn down.

title: Milton invented pandemonium
body: John Milton coined Pandæmonium in Paradise Lost (1667) as the name of the capital of Hell, from Greek pan- (all) and daimon (spirit or demon). Today it means wild chaos.

q.prompt: Who invented the word 'pandemonium'?

rq.prompt: What was Pandæmonium in Paradise Lost?

why: 'All demons' sums up the chaos.

title: Serendipity came from a fairy tale
body: Horace Walpole coined serendipity in a 1754 letter, inspired by a Persian fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept making lucky discoveries by accident. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka.

q.prompt: What is 'Serendip'?
options: An old name for Sri Lanka

rq.prompt: Who coined 'serendipity'?

why: The princes found things they weren't looking for.

title: Dr Seuss gave us 'nerd'
body: The earliest known printed use of nerd is in Dr Seuss's 1950 book If I Ran the Zoo, as the name of an imaginary creature. Within a year or two, American teenagers were using it for a dull or studious person.

q.prompt: Where does 'nerd' first appear in print?

rq.prompt: In that book, what was a nerd?

why: Slang often borrows from popular culture.

title: 'Run' has the most meanings
body: When the Oxford English Dictionary revised its entry for run, the verb alone had 645 meanings, more than any other English word. 'Set' had previously held the record with about 430.

q.prompt: Which English word has the most meanings in the OED?

rq.prompt: About how many meanings does 'run' (the verb) have?

why: Short, everyday words pick up new uses constantly.

title: A dictionary once listed a ghost word
body: Webster's 1934 dictionary included 'dord', meaning density. It wasn't a real word: a note saying 'D or d' (abbreviations for density) was misread. It stayed in print for years before an editor noticed.

q.prompt: How did 'dord' get into a dictionary?

rq.prompt: What was 'dord' supposed to mean?

why: 'D or d' meant the abbreviation could be capital or lower case.

title: Esperanto was invented in 1887
body: Ophthalmologist L. L. Zamenhof published Esperanto in 1887, hoping a simple shared second language would ease conflict between peoples. Its grammar has no irregular verbs. Today it has an estimated hundreds of thousands to a few million speakers.

q.prompt: What was Esperanto designed for?

rq.prompt: What's unusual about Esperanto's verbs?

why: Regular rules make it quicker to learn.

title: Hawaiian uses just 13 letters
body: The Hawaiian alphabet has only five vowels and eight consonants, counting the ʻokina, a glottal stop. That's why Hawaiian words like 'humuhumunukunukuāpuaʻa' repeat so many of the same sounds.

q.prompt: How many letters does the Hawaiian alphabet have?

rq.prompt: What is the ʻokina?

why: Fewer sounds mean words tend to be longer.

title: Basque is related to no other language
body: Basque, spoken in parts of northern Spain and southwest France, is a language isolate: it has no proven relatives. It was probably spoken in the region before Indo-European languages like Latin arrived.

q.prompt: Which European language has no known relatives?

rq.prompt: Where is Basque spoken?

why: It survived as other languages spread around it.

title: Papua New Guinea has over 800 languages
body: Papua New Guinea, with about 10 million people, has around 840 living languages, more than any other country. Mountains, jungles and islands kept communities separate for thousands of years.

q.prompt: Which country has the most languages?

rq.prompt: Why does PNG have so many languages?

why: Isolation lets languages drift apart.

source.name: Wikipedia: Languages of Papua New Guinea

title: A sentence made only of 'buffalo'
body: 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' is a grammatical sentence. It uses buffalo as a city, an animal and a verb meaning to bully: bison from Buffalo that other Buffalo bison bully, themselves bully Buffalo bison.

q.prompt: Can a sentence of only the word 'buffalo' be grammatical?

rq.prompt: What does the verb 'buffalo' mean?

why: One word playing three roles makes it work.
