title: Misheard lyrics are mondegreens
body: Writer Sylvia Wright coined mondegreen in 1954. As a child she'd heard a ballad line 'laid him on the green' as 'Lady Mondegreen'. Now the word covers any misheard phrase or song lyric.

q.prompt: What's a mondegreen?

rq.prompt: What line did Sylvia Wright mishear?

why: Our brains fill unclear sounds with familiar words.

title: Eggcorns are clever mistakes
body: An eggcorn is a mistaken word that still makes some sense, like 'egg corn' for acorn, or 'for all intensive purposes' for 'intents and purposes'. Linguists named them in 2003 after the acorn example.

q.prompt: Which is an eggcorn?

rq.prompt: What was the original eggcorn?

why: The mistaken version sounds plausible, so it spreads.

title: Repeat a word and it goes strange
body: Say a word like 'spoon' over and over and it soon feels meaningless and odd. This is semantic satiation. The brain's response to the word fades with repetition, briefly loosening the link between sound and meaning.

q.prompt: What happens when you repeat a word many times?

rq.prompt: What's this effect called?

why: Neural responses dampen when a stimulus repeats.

title: Tip of the tongue
body: When a word is on the tip of your tongue, you often know its first letter, number of syllables or similar-sounding words. Research suggests these moments become more frequent with age and are usually resolved within minutes.

q.prompt: In a tip-of-the-tongue moment, what do people often recall?

rq.prompt: How do these moments change with age?

why: Meaning is retrieved but the sound form is only partly reached.

title: The uncanny valley
body: In 1970, roboticist Masahiro Mori proposed that as robots look more human we like them more, until they become almost but not quite human. Then they turn creepy. He called that dip the uncanny valley.

q.prompt: Why might a very lifelike robot feel creepy?
options: It's almost but not quite human

rq.prompt: Who proposed the uncanny valley?

why: Small flaws in near-human faces may signal something is wrong.

title: The Ship of Theseus
body: If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship? And if you rebuilt the old planks into a second ship, which is the original? Plutarch recorded the puzzle nearly 2,000 years ago, and it still fuels debates about identity.

q.prompt: What does the Ship of Theseus puzzle ask about?
options: Whether something stays the same if all its parts change

rq.prompt: Who recorded the puzzle?

why: Your body's cells are also replaced over time.

title: Occam's razor
body: Occam's razor, named after the 14th-century friar William of Ockham, advises: don't add more assumptions than you need. When two explanations fit the facts equally well, prefer the simpler one. It's a guide, not a proof.

q.prompt: What does Occam's razor suggest?

rq.prompt: Is Occam's razor a proof?
options: No, it's a rule of thumb

why: Each extra assumption is another chance to be wrong.

title: Hanlon's razor
body: Hanlon's razor says: never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by carelessness or mistake. It's a reminder that most frustrating situations come from people being busy or wrong, not plotting against you.

q.prompt: Hanlon's razor suggests most annoying events are due to…

rq.prompt: What is it a useful reminder for?

why: Assuming malice often makes conflicts worse.

title: Achilles can't catch the tortoise?
body: Zeno of Elea argued that fast Achilles can never overtake a tortoise with a head start: each time he reaches where it was, it has moved on a bit. Mathematicians later resolved it: infinitely many shrinking steps can add up to a finite distance.

q.prompt: What resolves Zeno's Achilles paradox?
options: Infinite steps can sum to a finite distance

rq.prompt: Who devised the paradox?

why: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … adds up to exactly 1.

title: The trolley problem began in 1967
body: Philosopher Philippa Foot posed the trolley problem in 1967: should you divert a runaway tram to kill one person instead of five? It's used to explore the difference between doing harm and allowing it, and now informs debates about self-driving cars.

q.prompt: Who first posed the trolley problem?

rq.prompt: Which modern technology revived the debate?

why: Cars may need rules for unavoidable crash choices.

title: Socrates wrote nothing
body: Socrates, one of the founders of Western philosophy, never wrote anything down that survives. We know his ideas mainly through his students, especially Plato, whose dialogues star Socrates as the main speaker.

q.prompt: How do we know what Socrates thought?

rq.prompt: Which student wrote dialogues starring Socrates?

why: Socrates preferred live conversation to writing.

title: I think, therefore I am
body: René Descartes wanted one belief he couldn't doubt. Even if he doubted everything, he realised the act of doubting proved he existed. He wrote it in French in 1637 as 'je pense, donc je suis', later famous in Latin as 'cogito, ergo sum'.

q.prompt: What couldn't Descartes doubt?
options: That he existed, since he was thinking

rq.prompt: In which language did Descartes first publish the phrase?

why: Doubting is itself a kind of thinking.

title: Stoics split what you can control
body: The Stoic teacher Epictetus, a former slave, taught that some things are up to us, like our judgements and actions, and some aren't, like weather or others' opinions. Focusing only on the first brings peace of mind.

q.prompt: What did Epictetus say to focus on?

rq.prompt: What was Epictetus's background?

why: Worrying about uncontrollable things only adds suffering.

title: The prisoner's dilemma
body: Two suspects can each stay silent or betray the other. Betrayal looks best individually, but if both betray, both do worse than if both had stayed silent. The puzzle, devised in 1950, shows how self-interest can backfire.

q.prompt: In the prisoner's dilemma, what happens if both betray each other?
options: Both do worse than if both stayed silent

rq.prompt: What does the dilemma illustrate?

why: Trust lets both sides reach the better outcome.

title: The tragedy of the commons
body: If a pasture is shared by everyone, each herder gains by adding one more cow, but if all do, the grass is destroyed. Ecologist Garrett Hardin popularised the idea in 1968. Economist Elinor Ostrom later showed communities often manage commons well.

q.prompt: Who showed communities can manage shared resources well?

rq.prompt: What is the 'tragedy' of the commons?
options: Individual gain ruins a shared resource

why: Ostrom won a Nobel in economics in 2009 for this work.

title: Goodhart's law
body: Economist Charles Goodhart noted that measures used as targets stop being good measures. Paraphrased: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' People game the number instead of improving the real thing.

q.prompt: What happens when a measure becomes a target?
options: It stops being a good measure

rq.prompt: Why does Goodhart's law happen?

why: Effort shifts to hitting the metric, not the goal.

title: The 80/20 rule
body: Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto observed around 1900 that about 80% of Italy's land was owned by about 20% of the people. The 'Pareto principle' now loosely describes how a small share of causes often drives most of the effects.

q.prompt: What did Pareto originally observe?

rq.prompt: Is 80/20 an exact law?

why: Many real-world distributions are lopsided.

title: Survivorship bias
body: In the Second World War, statistician Abraham Wald studied damage on returning bombers. Rather than armouring where bullet holes clustered, he argued for armouring where returning planes had none, since planes hit there didn't come back.

q.prompt: Where did Wald suggest adding armour?
options: Where returning planes had no holes

rq.prompt: What error does survivorship bias describe?
options: Looking only at those who made it

why: The missing planes held the important information.

title: The Streisand effect
body: In 2003, Barbra Streisand sued to remove an aerial photo of her Malibu home from a coastal survey website. The lawsuit drew huge attention and the photo was viewed far more. Trying to hide something often spreads it.

q.prompt: What's the Streisand effect?
options: Trying to hide something makes it spread

rq.prompt: What did Streisand want removed?
options: An aerial photo of her home

why: Attention attracts curiosity.

title: The sunk cost fallacy
body: Sitting through a terrible film because you've paid for the ticket is the sunk cost fallacy. Money or time already spent can't be recovered, so it shouldn't decide what you do next; only future costs and benefits should.

q.prompt: Should money already spent decide what you do next?
options: No, only future costs and benefits

rq.prompt: What's an example of the sunk cost fallacy?
options: Finishing a bad film because you paid

why: Past costs are gone whatever you choose.

title: We notice what we already believe
body: Confirmation bias is our tendency to seek out, remember and trust information that supports what we already think, and to brush aside what doesn't. Deliberately looking for evidence against your view helps counter it.

q.prompt: What is confirmation bias?
options: Favouring evidence that fits our beliefs

rq.prompt: How can you counter it?
options: Look for evidence against your view

why: Agreeing evidence feels good; disagreeing evidence feels like a threat.

title: Chesterton's fence
body: G. K. Chesterton imagined a reformer finding a fence across a road and wanting it removed. A wiser one says: first find out why it was built. Only remove a rule or tradition once you understand its purpose.

q.prompt: What does Chesterton's fence advise?
options: Understand why something exists before removing it

rq.prompt: Who came up with the idea?

why: Old rules sometimes solve problems we've forgotten.

title: Parkinson's law
body: In a 1955 Economist essay, historian C. Northcote Parkinson wrote that 'work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion'. Give a task a week and it tends to take a week. Tighter deadlines can help.

q.prompt: According to Parkinson's law, work expands to fill…

rq.prompt: Where was Parkinson's law first published?

why: Without a deadline, tasks absorb extra polishing and delay.

title: Hofstadter's law
body: Douglas Hofstadter's playful law says: 'It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's law.' It captures our persistent tendency to underestimate how long tasks take, known as the planning fallacy.

q.prompt: What does Hofstadter's law say?
options: Things take longer than expected, even allowing for that

rq.prompt: What's the general tendency called?

why: We imagine the best case and forget surprises.

title: The map is not the territory
body: Philosopher Alfred Korzybski warned that a map, or any model, is not the reality it describes. Maps leave things out and can be out of date. The idea reminds us that our mental models are simplifications.

q.prompt: What does 'the map is not the territory' mean?
options: Models aren't the reality they describe

rq.prompt: Who coined the phrase?

why: Every model leaves something out.

title: Invert, always invert
body: Mathematician Carl Jacobi advised solving hard problems by turning them around. Investor Charlie Munger made it famous: instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid that.

q.prompt: What does 'inversion' suggest?
options: Ask what would cause failure, then avoid it

rq.prompt: Which mathematician said 'invert, always invert'?

why: Mistakes are often easier to spot than perfect plans.

title: Opportunity cost
body: The true cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up to make it. An evening spent scrolling costs whatever else you could have done with those hours. Economists call this opportunity cost.

q.prompt: What is the opportunity cost of a choice?
options: The best alternative you gave up

rq.prompt: Spending an evening on your phone has an opportunity cost of…

why: Time and money spent on one thing can't be spent on another.

title: Starry Night was painted from an asylum
body: Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in 1889 while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in southern France. It shows the view from his window just before sunrise, with an imagined village added.

q.prompt: Where was Van Gogh when he painted The Starry Night?

rq.prompt: What part of the painting did he imagine?

why: He painted from memory and imagination as well as the view.

title: Michelangelo painted standing up
body: Popular images show Michelangelo lying on his back to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling. In fact he worked standing on a scaffold he designed, painting overhead for four years, from 1508 to 1512. He wrote a poem complaining about the strain on his neck.

q.prompt: How did Michelangelo paint the Sistine ceiling?

rq.prompt: How long did the ceiling take?

why: The 'lying down' image comes from later fiction and films.

title: The Scream comes in several versions
body: Edvard Munch created The Scream in several versions: a painting from 1893, another from 1910, two pastels and a run of prints. The 1895 pastel sold in 2012 for nearly $120 million.

q.prompt: How many versions of The Scream did Munch make?

rq.prompt: Which country was Edvard Munch from?

why: Artists often revisited their most powerful images.

title: The golden ratio myth
body: Books often claim the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa and the Great Pyramid were built on the golden ratio, about 1.618. Careful measurements don't support most of these claims, and studies find people don't reliably prefer golden rectangles.

q.prompt: Was the Parthenon designed around the golden ratio?

rq.prompt: Roughly what is the golden ratio?

why: With enough points to choose from, you can find any ratio in a building.

title: Blue paint once cost more than gold
body: Ultramarine, the deepest blue of Renaissance paintings, was made by grinding lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan. It could be more expensive than gold, so patrons sometimes specified in contracts how much ultramarine a painter must use, often for the Virgin Mary's robes.

q.prompt: What was Renaissance ultramarine made from?

rq.prompt: Where was the lapis lazuli mined?

why: 'Ultramarine' means 'beyond the sea', where it came from.

title: One of the blackest materials
body: Vantablack, developed by Surrey NanoSystems, is a coating of tiny carbon nanotubes that absorbs about 99.96% of visible light. Coated objects look like holes. Artist Anish Kapoor holds exclusive rights to use it in art, which caused an art-world feud.

q.prompt: How much visible light does Vantablack absorb?

rq.prompt: Which artist holds exclusive art rights to Vantablack?

why: Light gets trapped bouncing between the nanotubes.

title: Beethoven composed while deaf
body: Beethoven began losing his hearing in his late twenties and was almost completely deaf by the time he wrote his Ninth Symphony, premiered in 1824. At its end, a musician reportedly turned him round so he could see the applause.

q.prompt: Was Beethoven deaf when he wrote his Ninth Symphony?

rq.prompt: When was the Ninth Symphony first performed?

why: He could still 'hear' music in his imagination.

title: Happy Birthday is now free to sing
body: 'Happy Birthday to You' was long claimed under copyright, earning millions in licence fees. In 2015 a US court ruled the copyright claim invalid, and in 2016 the song was officially placed in the public domain.

q.prompt: Is 'Happy Birthday to You' still under copyright in the US?

rq.prompt: What ended the copyright claim?

why: The court found no valid evidence of a copyright on the lyrics.

title: Mozart wrote a symphony at eight
body: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed his first symphony in 1764 in London, aged about eight. By then he had already toured Europe as a child performer. He wrote over 600 works before dying at 35.

q.prompt: How old was Mozart when he wrote his first symphony?

rq.prompt: Where did Mozart write his first symphony?

why: His father Leopold trained him intensively from early childhood.

title: A4 paper halves perfectly
body: A-series paper has sides in the ratio 1 to √2. Fold an A4 sheet in half and you get A5 with exactly the same shape. A0 is defined as one square metre, so A4 is a sixteenth of that.

q.prompt: What's special about A4 paper's shape?
options: Halving it keeps the same shape

rq.prompt: What area is A0 paper?

why: The √2 ratio is the only one that keeps its shape when halved.

title: Zero as a number came from India
body: Many cultures had a symbol for 'nothing here' in their numbers, but Indian mathematicians treated zero as a number in its own right. In 628, Brahmagupta wrote rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero.

q.prompt: Where was zero first treated as a number with its own rules?

rq.prompt: Which mathematician wrote early rules for zero?

why: Treating 'nothing' as a number made algebra far easier.

title: Fibonacci brought our digits to Europe
body: Europe used Roman numerals until Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, promoted Hindu-Arabic digits in his 1202 book Liber Abaci. He had learned them while growing up in North Africa. Merchants found them far easier for calculation.

q.prompt: Who promoted Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe in 1202?

rq.prompt: Where did Fibonacci learn the numerals?

why: Try doing long multiplication in Roman numerals.

title: The birthday paradox
body: In a group of just 23 people, there's a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday. It feels wrong because we think about our own birthday, but the number of possible pairs grows fast: 23 people make 253 pairs.

q.prompt: How many people make a shared birthday more likely than not?

rq.prompt: How many pairs are there among 23 people?

why: Pairs, not individuals, are what match.

title: Switch doors in the Monty Hall problem
body: Pick one of three doors; a car is behind one. The host, who knows where it is, opens another door showing a goat and offers a switch. Switching wins two-thirds of the time. Even some mathematicians refused to believe it at first.

q.prompt: Should you switch doors in the Monty Hall problem?
options: Yes, it wins 2/3 of the time

rq.prompt: Why does switching help?
options: The host's choice gives you information

why: Your first pick was right only 1/3 of the time.

title: Some infinities are bigger than others
body: In the 1870s Georg Cantor proved that the infinity of all real numbers is larger than the infinity of whole numbers: you can't pair them up one-to-one. It shocked mathematicians, and some fiercely opposed him.

q.prompt: Can one infinity be bigger than another?

rq.prompt: Who proved it?

why: There's always a real number left over in any list.

title: Benford's law
body: In many real-world data sets, from populations to bills, the leading digit is 1 about 30% of the time and 9 less than 5%. Auditors use this pattern, called Benford's law, to spot fabricated numbers.

q.prompt: In many real data sets, how often does the first digit equal 1?

rq.prompt: Who uses Benford's law to detect fraud?

why: Made-up numbers tend to have evenly spread first digits.

title: NASA needs only 15 digits of pi
body: Pi's digits go on forever without repeating. But NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory says it uses about 15 decimal places for interplanetary navigation. With 40 digits you could calculate the circumference of the observable universe to within an atom's width.

q.prompt: How many decimal places of pi does NASA's JPL typically use?

rq.prompt: Do pi's digits ever repeat in a pattern?

why: Extra digits make errors smaller than anything measurable.

source.name: NASA JPL: How many decimals of pi do we really need?

title: Six degrees of separation
body: In 1967, Stanley Milgram asked people in the US Midwest to pass a letter to a stranger in Boston via acquaintances. Letters that arrived took about six steps on average. Later studies of online networks found similarly short chains.

q.prompt: How many steps did Milgram's letters take on average?

rq.prompt: What does 'six degrees of separation' suggest?
options: Everyone is linked by short chains

why: A few well-connected people link distant groups.

title: Dunbar's number
body: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar proposed that humans can keep around 150 stable relationships, linked to the size of our brains' neocortex. The exact number is debated, but similar group sizes appear in villages, armies and companies.

q.prompt: About how many stable relationships did Dunbar propose we can keep?

rq.prompt: Is Dunbar's number exact?

why: Tracking who's who in a group takes brainpower.

title: Tycoon, shampoo and pyjamas are borrowed
body: English borrows from everywhere. Tycoon comes from the Japanese taikun, a title for a great lord. Shampoo comes from Hindi chāmpo, to press or massage. Pyjamas come from Persian and Urdu words for leg garment.

q.prompt: Which language gave English 'shampoo'?

rq.prompt: What did 'tycoon' originally mean?

why: Trade and empire brought words home with goods.

title: Avocado, chocolate and tomato are Nahuatl
body: These words come from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, through Spanish: avocado from āhuacatl, tomato from tomatl, and chocolate probably from a Nahuatl word for a drink. Chilli and coyote too.

q.prompt: Which language gave us 'tomato' and 'avocado'?

rq.prompt: Who spoke Nahuatl?

why: Spanish explorers borrowed names along with the foods.

title: The ampersand is a squashed 'and'
body: The symbol & started as a joined-up Latin et, meaning and. Children reciting the alphabet once ended with '…X, Y, Z, and per se and', meaning '& by itself is and'. Slurred together, that became ampersand.

q.prompt: What Latin word is the & symbol based on?

rq.prompt: Where does the name 'ampersand' come from?
options: 'And per se and' in alphabet recitals

why: & was once taught as the 27th letter of the alphabet.

title: Emoji has nothing to do with emotion
body: Emoji is Japanese: e means picture, and moji means written character. The resemblance to 'emotion' is a coincidence. Shigetaka Kurita designed an influential early set of 176 emoji for a Japanese mobile service in 1999.

q.prompt: What does 'emoji' mean in Japanese?

rq.prompt: Who designed an influential early emoji set in 1999?

why: The similarity to 'emotion' helped the word spread.

title: 'Typewriter' fits on one row
body: 'Typewriter' is famously one of the longest common English words you can type using only the top row of letters on a QWERTY keyboard. Try it: every letter is between Q and P.

q.prompt: Which word can you type using only the top letter row?

rq.prompt: Which keyboard layout does this apply to?

why: The top row includes T, Y, P, E, W, R and I.

title: Writing was invented more than once
body: Writing seems to have been invented independently at least three or four times: in Mesopotamia around 3200 BC, in China by about 1200 BC, and in Mesoamerica by about 500 BC, with Egypt's hieroglyphs possibly a separate case.

q.prompt: Was writing invented only once?

rq.prompt: Where did the earliest known writing appear?

why: Growing cities needed records of trade and taxes.

title: The first writing was accounting
body: The earliest cuneiform tablets from the city of Uruk, in today's Iraq, mostly record grain, livestock and labour. Writing seems to have started as bookkeeping long before it was used for stories or poems.

q.prompt: What did most of the earliest writing record?

rq.prompt: What was the earliest writing system called?

why: Temples needed to track who owed what.

title: Ancient Greek had no spaces
body: Ancient Greek and Latin were often written in scriptio continua: no spaces between words, little punctuation and no lowercase letters. Readers usually read aloud to work out where words began and ended.

q.prompt: How was ancient Greek usually written?

rq.prompt: How did readers cope?
options: They used spaces in their heads only

why: Word spacing spread later, partly through Irish and English monks.

title: Nobody knows where 'dog' came from
body: Dog is one of English's great etymological mysteries. It appears in late Old English as docga, probably first for a particular breed, while the usual word was hund (hound). Linguists still don't know where docga came from.

q.prompt: Do we know where the word 'dog' comes from?

rq.prompt: What was the usual Old English word for dog?

why: Some words appear without a clear ancestor.

title: Spoonerisms
body: Swapping the first sounds of words, like 'a blushing crow' for 'a crushing blow', is called a spoonerism. It's named after William Archibald Spooner, an Oxford don famous for such slips, though many quotes attributed to him were invented by students.

q.prompt: What is a spoonerism?
options: Swapping the first sounds of words

rq.prompt: Who are spoonerisms named after?

why: The brain sometimes plans sounds ahead and mixes them up.

title: Palindromes read both ways
body: A palindrome reads the same backwards and forwards, ignoring spaces and punctuation. Classics include 'racecar' and 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'. The word comes from the Greek palindromos, running back again.

q.prompt: Which of these is a palindrome?
options: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
To be or not to be

rq.prompt: What does the Greek root of 'palindrome' mean?

why: Its letters mirror around the centre.

title: The 'fifty words for snow' myth
body: The claim that Inuit languages have dozens of words for snow is misleading. These languages build long words from many parts, so one root can make endless forms. By that counting, English has many snow words too: slush, sleet, powder, blizzard, drift.

q.prompt: Is the 'Inuit have 50 words for snow' claim accurate?

rq.prompt: Why can Inuit languages form so many snow terms?
options: They build long words from many parts

why: How you count 'words' changes the answer.

title: Cappuccino is named after friars
body: Cappuccino takes its name from the Capuchin friars, whose brown hooded robes matched the colour of coffee mixed with milk. The friars' name itself comes from cappuccio, the Italian for hood.

q.prompt: Who is cappuccino named after?

rq.prompt: What does Italian 'cappuccio' mean?

why: The milky coffee matched their robes.

title: 'Sincere' doesn't mean 'without wax'
body: A popular story says sincere comes from Latin sine cera, 'without wax', because honest sculptors didn't hide cracks with wax. It's a myth. The word comes from Latin sincerus, meaning clean, pure or whole.

q.prompt: Does 'sincere' come from 'without wax'?

rq.prompt: What does Latin 'sincerus' mean?

why: Neat stories often attach themselves to words later.

title: 'Posh' doesn't mean 'port out, starboard home'
body: The tale that posh came from tickets stamped P.O.S.H., for the shaded cabins on voyages to India, is a myth. No such tickets have been found, and the acronym story only appeared decades after the word. Its true origin is unknown.

q.prompt: Did 'posh' come from 'port out, starboard home'?

rq.prompt: Is the real origin of 'posh' known?

why: Acronym origins for old words are almost always invented.

title: 'Rule of thumb' isn't about beating wives
body: A story claims old English law allowed a man to beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb. Historians have found no such law. The phrase most likely comes from using your thumb as a rough measuring tool.

q.prompt: Did 'rule of thumb' come from a law about beating?
options: No, there's no evidence of such a law
It came from carpentry rules only

rq.prompt: What's the likely origin of 'rule of thumb'?
options: Using the thumb to measure roughly

why: An inch was once roughly a thumb's width.

title: Plato's cave
body: In Plato's allegory, prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows on a wall and think they're reality. One escapes, sees the real world in sunlight, and returns to tell the others, who don't believe him. It's about education and how we know what's real.

q.prompt: In Plato's cave, what do the prisoners mistake for reality?

rq.prompt: What happens when the escaped prisoner returns?

why: Plato meant learning can feel painful and be resisted.

title: Diogenes lived in a jar
body: The Greek philosopher Diogenes rejected comfort and convention, reportedly living in a large ceramic jar in Athens. When Alexander the Great offered him any favour, Diogenes is said to have asked him to stand out of his sunlight.

q.prompt: What did Diogenes reportedly ask Alexander the Great?
options: To stand out of his sunlight

rq.prompt: Where did Diogenes reportedly live?

why: He believed needing little made you free.

title: Confucius's version of the golden rule
body: Long before many later versions, Confucius taught: 'Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself.' Similar principles appear across many religions and philosophies worldwide.

q.prompt: What did Confucius say about treating others?
options: Don't do to others what you wouldn't want

rq.prompt: Is the golden rule unique to one culture?

why: Empathy-based ethics arose independently in many places.

title: Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great
body: Around 343 BC, King Philip II of Macedon hired the philosopher Aristotle to tutor his 13-year-old son, the future Alexander the Great. He taught him for several years, covering subjects from ethics to medicine.

q.prompt: Who tutored the young Alexander the Great?

rq.prompt: How old was Alexander when the tutoring began?

why: Philip wanted the best mind in Greece for his heir.

title: Kant's famously regular walks
body: Philosopher Immanuel Kant lived his whole life in and around Königsberg. He was so regular in his habits that, according to a popular story, neighbours could set their clocks by his afternoon walk.

q.prompt: What were Kant's neighbours said to set clocks by?

rq.prompt: Where did Kant spend nearly all his life?

why: Strict routine left his mind free for hard thinking.

title: The 'Mozart effect' is mostly a myth
body: A 1993 study found students did slightly better on a spatial task right after hearing Mozart. It was hyped as 'Mozart makes babies smarter'. Later research found the small effect was short-lived, and likely came from music lifting mood and alertness.

q.prompt: Does listening to Mozart make you smarter long-term?

rq.prompt: What likely caused the brief effect?

why: Any enjoyable music had similar effects in later studies.

title: The pangram that uses every letter
body: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' contains every letter of the English alphabet. Sentences like this, called pangrams, were used to test typewriters and to show off fonts.

q.prompt: What's special about 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'?

rq.prompt: What is a sentence using every letter called?

why: It checks every key on a keyboard.

source.name: Wikipedia: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog

title: 'Rhythms' has no standard vowels
body: Rhythms is one of the longest common English words without a, e, i, o or u. The letter y does the vowel's job. Other examples include crypt, gym and myths.

q.prompt: Which word has no a, e, i, o or u?

rq.prompt: Which letter acts as the vowel in 'rhythms'?

why: Y can be a consonant or a vowel depending on the word.

title: Anagrams hid scientific discoveries
body: In 1610 Galileo announced a discovery about Saturn as a scrambled anagram, so he could claim priority without revealing it. Christiaan Huygens later did the same for Saturn's rings. Rivals had to wait for the unscrambled answer.

q.prompt: Why did Galileo publish a discovery as an anagram?
options: To claim credit without revealing it

rq.prompt: Which planet were these anagrams about?

why: A scrambled message proved who found it first.

title: The Oxford comma
body: The Oxford comma is the optional comma before 'and' in a list. Compare 'I thanked my parents, Ayesha and God' with 'I thanked my parents, Ayesha, and God'. Without it, the sentence can suggest your parents are Ayesha and God.

q.prompt: Where does the Oxford comma go?
options: Before 'and' at the end of a list
At the start of a sentence

rq.prompt: Why do fans like the Oxford comma?

why: In 2017 a US court case over overtime pay turned on a missing serial comma.

title: Shakespeare's words
body: Shakespeare is the earliest recorded source for hundreds of English words and phrases, such as 'eyeball' and 'swagger'. Some were probably already in speech, but his plays spread them widely and many stuck.

q.prompt: Did Shakespeare invent every word first recorded in his plays?
options: Not necessarily, some were already spoken

rq.prompt: Which word has an early recorded use in Shakespeare?

why: Dictionaries record first written uses, not first spoken ones.

title: Hello took off with the telephone
body: Hello existed before phones, but it was mainly used to attract attention or express surprise. Thomas Edison championed it as the standard way to answer the telephone in the late 1870s. Alexander Graham Bell preferred 'ahoy'.

q.prompt: What did Alexander Graham Bell want people to say when answering the phone?

rq.prompt: Who championed 'hello' for the phone?

why: Edison's choice spread with telephone exchanges.

title: Writing on wet clay
body: Cuneiform, meaning wedge-shaped, was written by pressing a cut reed into wet clay. Tablets were cheap and, once baked, nearly indestructible. Ironically, fires that destroyed ancient libraries often baked their tablets, preserving them.

q.prompt: What did cuneiform writers write on?

rq.prompt: How did fires sometimes help preserve tablets?

why: Baked clay can last thousands of years.

title: The # has a fancy name
body: The # symbol has many names: hash, pound sign, number sign. Engineers at Bell Labs in the 1960s gave it a playful official name, octothorpe, for the new touch-tone phone keypads. Several stories compete to explain the 'thorpe'.

q.prompt: What did Bell Labs engineers call the # symbol?

rq.prompt: What was it named for?

why: 'Octo' refers to its eight ends.

title: The Voynich manuscript is unreadable
body: The Voynich manuscript is a 15th-century book full of strange plants and an unknown script. Radiocarbon dating places its vellum in the early 1400s. Despite efforts by codebreakers, nobody has convincingly deciphered it.

q.prompt: Has the Voynich manuscript been deciphered?

rq.prompt: When was the Voynich manuscript's vellum dated to?

why: Its script matches no known language or code.

title: The Library of Babel
body: Jorge Luis Borges imagined an endless library holding every possible book of a certain length, every combination of letters. Somewhere in it is the true story of your life, and countless almost-true versions. It's a famous thought experiment on meaning and infinity.

q.prompt: What does Borges' Library of Babel contain?

rq.prompt: Who wrote The Library of Babel?

why: Having everything is useless if you can't find the meaningful bits.

title: Learning works best with spacing
body: You're using it right now. Decades of research show that spreading reviews over days and weeks, and testing yourself rather than re-reading, leads to far better long-term memory than cramming. Little and often beats a lot at once.

q.prompt: Which leads to better long-term memory?

rq.prompt: What's this effect called?

why: Each time you nearly forget and then recall, the memory strengthens.
